speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister of Agriculture if he is in a position this morning to tell the house in a general way the contents of the report which I understand he

Inquiries of the Ministry has received concerning the tragic crop situation in the Peace river country, and to let us know what measures his department proposes to take to help relieve the situation there.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON INVESTIGATION INTO HARVEST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there has been a very unfortunate situation this year from the point of view of weather in the Peace river country. I sent a special investigation team into the area some two weeks ago to make a report on the exact situation that existed there, with a view to seeing whether the crop situation was such that although no threshing had taken place in a large number of places it would be possible to put into effect P.F.A.A. payments.
The report I received was that approximately only 30 per cent of the threshing had been done in the Peace river area including the British Columbia block, and that it was extremely doubtful whether more than something between 10 per cent and 20 per cent of the remaining grain would ever be threshed. In view of those circumstances I issued instructions that something between 40 and 50 P.F.A.A. inspectors should be secured immediately to make a detailed assessment of the situation in practically every township in the Peace river area. As a result of this I expect that P.F.A.A. payments in very considerable amounts will be put into effect in the area.
In addition, the crop which was harvested in the Peace river country was nearly all tough and damp grain. Therefore representations were made that if this grain was to be saved and prevented from going bad, special means would have to be taken in order to get it down to a terminal elevator where it could be dried. I took up this matter with the wheat board and the Department of Trade and Commerce. They are now working on that problem, and I trust that some means will be evolved of getting this grain into the terminal elevator in Edmonton and possibly the terminal elevator at Vancouver, where it can be dried and thus made available for general use.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. M. Macdonnell (Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: REPORTED SLOWNESS IN PROVIDING ADDITIONAL QUOTAS

Mr. Speaker, it is the policy of the Canadian wheat board to increase delivery quotas as rapidly as possible. The hon. member will appreciate, however, that before a delivery quota can be increased some space must be accumulated to take care of at least a part of the increase. This is particularly true at larger delivery points, where an increase of 1 bushel per specified acre requires a relatively large amount of space. Bearing upon the question of the hon. member is the fact that at a considerable number of delivery points in the prairie provinces there is some space available but not sufficient to take care of all the grain which producers can deliver

Inquiries of the Ministry under present delivery quotas. It will not be the policy of the board to hold this space for any length of time.
The present country elevator stocks of grain are 305 million bushels as compared with 296 million bushels at the same time last year. I can assure the hon. member that the wheat board will continue to increase delivery quotas just as rapidly as space permits.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Fisheries and ask him whether he has received representations from the Shelburne and other county ministerial associations, requesting that the opening of the lobster season in district No. 4 be changed from Sunday, December 1, to Tuesday, December 3? speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacLean (Minisler of Fisheries):
subtopic: LOBSTER DISTRICT NO. 4, N.S.-OPENING OF SEASON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for giving me notice of his intention to ask this question. I think the correct answer is yes, but I cannot be specific about this particular ministerial association. In any case, such a representation has been made by several ministerial associations, including that of Queens county, Nova Scotia. I might say that the hon. member for Queens-Lunen-burg (Mr. Crouse) has already discussed the same matter with me and had indicated his intention to ask a similar question.
A request was received on November 21 from the Queens county ministerial association that the Department of Fisheries investigate the matter immediately and, if possible, to take the necessary steps to change the opening date of the lobster season in this area for this year from December 1 to December 3. The lobster fishermen would thus be allowed to set their traps on Monday, December 2, instead of Saturday, November 30. Since the opening has already been advertised as effective December 1, it would be rather difficult to effect any change this year.
I might point out however, Mr. Speaker, that existing regulations permit lobster fishermen to set their traps on the noon of the preceding Saturday when the opening date falls on either a Sunday or a Monday.

This regulation was established pursuant to discussions between senior officials of the department and lobster fishermen throughout the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island; and I might point out that an overwhelming preference was expressed by the fishermen in favour of the existing regulation. Thus where the season opens on a Sunday, by reason of the fact that traps may be set on the Saturday preceding, the opening Sunday would be precisely the same as any other Sunday falling within the open season, and whether or not the traps are fished is left entirely to the discretion of the individual fisherman himself.
In other words, the decision is that the lobster fishermen can set their traps tomorrow, and that will result in Sunday being in exactly the same position as any other Sunday which falls within the lobster season.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. Brooks (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say at this time that I am very conscious of my responsibility in presenting the estimates for the current fiscal year, of the department 96698-106
Supply-Veterans Affairs whose duty it is to care for my former comrades and the dependants of those who gave their lies in the cause of freedom. I must ensure that the work of the department is carried on just as economically as is possible, but, at the same time insist that there be no downgrading of the several services that the department is required to render.
I welcome this opportunity to express publicly my appreciation of the co-operation I have received since taking office, from all members of the house, from the Canadian Legion, the national council of veterans associations in Canada, and other veteran organizations, from officials of the benevolent funds of the three armed services and from other organizations and individuals with whom the department is associated in its work. I assure you, Mr. Chairman, that this co-operation has rendered my task much easier.
As hon. members know, the main estimates of the department which are now before the committee were presented to the house by the former government, and were actually prepared by the department in October and November, 1956. The experience in the rate of expenditure for the first seven months of the current fiscal year indicates that there will be some reduction in the requirements estimated at that time. The organization of the department has remained unchanged during the past year and the establishment has reached a continuing level. There has been a decrease in the number of employees in practically every vote except treatment services. The increase in treatment services staff results mainly from the extension of the five-day week to all D.V.A. hospitals.
In spite of reductions in staff, all salary votes show an increase consequent upon the general salary revision effective May 1, 1957. Furthermore, taking the main and supplementary estimates together, the votes for pensions and war veterans allowances show increases resulting from the revision in rates and permissible income ceilings which were approved by the last parliament to be effective July 1, 1957.
Generally speaking, Mr. Chairman, the volume of work of the department has remained fairly constant, but it might be noted that the trend of the activity of the welfare services branch has continued to move away from work connected with rehabilitation benefits and toward the handling of war veterans allowance problems and individual welfare cases of a problem nature. The branch is successfully applying the provisions of the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act, and it is gratifying to note that the

Supply-Veterans Affairs number of applications has exceeded somewhat the number the department had expected. A total of 277 children have completed their training program, and 465 are undergoing training at the present.
The level of the treatment patient load remains steady. Construction continues with a view to bringing all D.V.A. hospitals to a modern standard. The construction at Colonel Belcher, Calgary, is now completed; that at Deer Lodge hospital near Winnipeg will be finished next spring; construction at Shaugh-nessy, Vancouver, has been started; and at Westminster hospital, London, Ontario, it is in the planning stage.
As hon. members know, the government, in the few months since it took ofiice has already been able to prepare two bills, one of which to amend the Pension Act is now before this house and the other, amending the War Veterans' Allowance Act, has already received the approval of this house and the Senate and has been given royal assent. Other acts are being studied, and where changes are necessary amending legislation will be introduced at an appropriate time in the future.
Before resuming my seat I should like to say a word about the Vimy memorial. As hon. members know, this is one of the most impressive monuments built after world war I. Though undamaged by enemy action, the Vimy memorial has suffered somewhat by lack of adequate maintenance care during the war years. Extensive renovation work is now being carried out and is expected to be completed by next spring. The work will restore the beauty of this outstanding memorial to Canada's dead.
I shall have more to say, Mr. Chairman, on the different items in the estimates as they come up for consideration. I shall also answer, as far as possible, any questions which hon. members may care to ask on the first item. I assume, following the ordinary procedure, there will be a general discussion. We have already had an extensive debate on the War Veterans' Allowance Act and a considerable debate on the resolution preceding the pension bill.

I do not intend to take too long at this stage, Mr. Chairman, because as the minister has stated most of the expenditures provided for in these estimates are expenditures authorized for pensions, war veterans allowance, treatment of veterans, Veterans' Land Act operations and the like. It is a matter of voting money for the splendid work being done by Canada for those who served in her armed services over the past many years. I have not heard the minister suggest that this is one of those departments in which there is waste or extravagance, reference to which has been made by

other members of the government concerning proposed expenditures in the estimates brought down by the previous government. I hope the minister will definitely indicate whether or not he has found any evidence of waste or extravagance in his department.
I have more knowledge of this department than other government departments, and I must say that if other departments are administered with similar devotion to the duty of the department under the statutes passed by this parliament and with the same attempt to do the best possible job of which human beings are capable, then I am sure we have the finest administration by the civil service of Canada of any country in the world. Sometimes it seems to me that people do not realize the tremendous amount of good work that is being done in this department. Again I say that I do not know very much about the other departments, but I do know that at times there is a feeling there are more civil servants than are necessary to do the work involved. I am not saying that is true, but I know some people believe it. If the same conditions prevail in other departments that prevail in the Department of Veterans Affairs, then I can say decisively the statement is not true.
The various persons involved in the administration of this department are really trying very hard to do their work in a conscientious way and to carry out the purposes parliament had in mind when it passed the veterans charter and the amendments which have been made thereto from time to time. Sometimes we do not realize the amount of very hard work and devoted service we get from our civil servants. I think these remarks, made at a time when I am now in the opposition, will probably be more fitting and carry more weight than those of a person who is a supporter of the government. I have known many men in that department who have worked to the point where I felt they were endangering their health in order to get a good job done.
If one looks through the report of the Department of Veterans Affairs and considers the number of people in Canada who are benefited by the work of that department I think, even if he has some knowledge of the work of the department, he must be astonished at the amount of work that is accomplished. For example, let us consider the payment of war service gratuities. There was actually paid out a sum totalling $470 million, not including payments to the Korean veterans. Payments to Korean veterans numbering 26,476 amounted to over $6.5 million, according to the last annual

report. Re-establishment credits, which helped so many veterans get re-established, totalled $299 million, not including the payments to Korean veterans. If we include the payments to Korean veterans the total is brought up to over $302 million.
There is another matter I should like to mention. The Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act was passed to ensure that the children of men who served their country and who were killed or disabled, do not suffer by virtue of that service. I am sure all hon. members approve of that measure, and personally I hope consideration will be given to expanding that act in order to see to it that when a person has lost his life or has been disabled in the service of his country, his children shall not suffer in any way shape or form having regard to the education they are able to get or the training they may get for life. In that regard the country should consider itself as stepping into the position of the parent who gave his service so unselfishly for his country. This work has gone on well but, as I say, study should be given to expanding it so as to make it apply not only to those who were killed but to those who were disabled.
As the minister knows, he and I have talked about this matter. I am sure he and his associates, the people in the department, are sympathetic to the idea I have put forward. I was pleased to see that even more advantage had been taken of this act providing for help to educate the children of the war dead than I think was expected at the time it was passed. I note that according to the annual report the total number who had been dealt with under that act is 872. When one considers what that means in the matter of helping the children of those who have served, one must be extremely glad that parliament has made that provision.
I should like to compliment the department on the work being done in connection with correspondence courses. I was glad to find that there were no less than some 9,500 being helped last year through correspondence courses under the Department of Veterans Affairs. Then I think of the welfare services, and I will not take the time of the house to go into that matter in any detail. However, that personal attention given to assisting veterans in their various problems and difficulties is something of which any one who knows anything of the work must be very proud and pleased.
The war veterans assistance fund, which was designed to help those people who could not supplement their incomes, also has been helpful and has been used, I think, more than
many hon. members realize. I note that according to the last annual report there were no less than 4,058 on the list receiving help as at March 31, 1956, and that the total number of those who had been helped during that year 1956-57 ran up to something over
8,000	who were in receipt of war veterans allowance but who needed additional help under that war veterans assistance fund.
As to the number of veterans under the War Veterans Allowance Act getting help, I have heard that act described by many people as an act which is perhaps rather unique with regard to veterans legislation. Many people regard it as a pension for disability or something of the sort but it is, in fact, an act designed to give assistance to those who are not pensioned or not getting adequate pensions to get along. Several countries which were our allies in the war have no such provision to assist their veterans. I know that war veterans generally consider that act to be one of the finest under the veterans charter. The war veterans allowance expenditure, as I see it in the estimates, is nearly $50 million.
Then I come to the treatment services. There again continuing treatment of those who were disabled, particularly those who are permanently disabled, is a work that is going on carefully and with some consideration for services rendered by those being treated. I think ex-servicemen are highly satisfied with the treatment they are getting in our veterans hospitals. I note that according to the report the number of patients in departmental hospitals as of March 31, 1957, was over 7,800. Actually the number of admissions to departmental hospitals during that year had been over 50,000, the number of admissions to other hospitals some 18,000, and the number of out-patient treatments some
657,000.
I should like to mention prosthetic services. I venture to say most hon. members have no idea of the amount of good work that is being done in that particular field. I note that according to the report the number of appliances supplied during the year was no less than 123,000, with 20,000 repairs, and that the total number of patients dealt with in connection with prosthetic services in the last year were no less than 69,000.
The veterans bureau is something that is, in my opinion, of great value. No doubt the various veterans organizations such as the Canadian Legion, the army and navy and air force veterans association, and the Canadian council of disabled veterans, have given great help to veterans in pressing for their pensions and other needed assistance. The veterans bureau is always there to give help

Supply-Veterans Affairs even where the Canadian Legion or other veterans organizations are willing to help. They may not be as well organized in one part of the country as in another. According to the annual report I note that the number of claims brought forward by the veterans bureau was 5,800. I think hon. members who have had anything to do with this work will realize the tremendous amount of work involved in preparing that number of cases for submission to the pension board.
There is one act to which I very much want to refer, and that is the Veterans' Land Act. Under the director of the Veterans' Land Act, Brigadier Rutherford, there has been set up a system of advising the veterans who are settled under the V.L.A., and of assisting them in being successful farmers, giving them the best scientific advice and the like, so the man who is the representative of the Veterans' Land Act I believe in most cases is regarded as the real friend of the veteran and not purely as a collector of outstanding accounts. The amount of good work done in enabling people to establish themselves in full time and part time farming, as evidenced by the number of happy and successful homes that have been set up as a result of this splendid legislation, is really something on which, in my opinion, we can look with a great deal of satisfaction.
I see in the annual report that $357 million had been expended on behalf of over 67,700 veterans, and I think hon. members can be very pleased that, up to March 31 this year, of the amount spent over a period of 12J years in settlement operations approximately 40 per cent has been paid by the veterans themselves. This shows that the legislation was conceived in such a way as to give our veterans a chance to be successful, and it is also an indication of good administration over the years. In this connection I would like to sincerely compliment the people engaged in this work.
I would also like to mention the work done by the department in connection with small holdings and the encouragement of veterans in the building of their own homes. They have been able to save a great deal of money in this way, and I think it has worked splendidly in enabling them to become home owners for much less money than would otherwise have been the case.
I would like to deal for a moment with the Pension Act. I am going through these details rather hurriedly, as I do not wish to hold up the proceedings in the house, but I feel quite strongly, having been in contact with the department for many years, that it would be unfair of me not to take the first opportunity to commend the people with whom I have


been associated in the department on the wonderful job they have done. I think the veterans of our country and the people of Canada generally do appreciate the good work done by the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Now in regard to disability pensions, I think the average member can have no conception of the amount of work done by the pension commission. Each case, of course, requires detailed examination and, although I do not say that pensions have always been granted where I personally may have thought they should have been granted, it has been the feeling of veterans that it is desirable to have the matter left in the hands of an independent pension commission which would not be under pressure from any person in government. In this way the matter is freed entirely from any question of political partisanship, and this is only fair to our veterans. This tradition has been established by the pension commissioners down through the years, and they have tried to do a completely non-partisan job. As a matter of fact I know that members sometimes get letters about pension matters from their constituents, who find it hard to believe that the member cannot in some way bring pressure to bear in this regard.
What the member can do and in fact does -and this is welcomed by the commission- is to bring forward all the facts and arguments he can on behalf of the veteran. My own experience has been that these cases are given very sympathetic consideration, but there the matter stops so far as any influencing of the commission is concerned. The tradition has been established, and they decide as they think right in the light of the terms of the act provided for them by parliament. I am sure the people of Canada and parliament would wish this to be so.
According to the annual report I see that disability pensions in force at March 31, 1957, numbered 54,400 with respect to world war I. Pensions paid in respect of dependents numbered over 15,000. Payments in respect of disability went to dependents numbering 69,400. The grand total in receipt of benefits totalled over 114,000. This is in respect of world war I. This involves a tremendous amount of work, and one wonders how the people who have done this work over the years have managed to accomplish as much as they have.
With respect to world war I, their numbers are unfortunately dwindling. I believe the falling off in the number of people in receipt of pensions with respect to world war I totalled somewhere around 2,000 during last

year. As the country sees the people who served it in war passing from their midst, I am sure they will be glad that at least as much has been done for them as has in fact been done; and will certainly feel that in all fairness if there is some further improvement which can be made it should be given sympathetic consideration.
With respect to world war II, of course, the department has been more active in connection with application for pensions and so on, and I see that the total number of pensions in force with respect to this war as at March 31, 1957, was 120,700. This again involves a tremendous amount of detail work, important as it is. I have not spent much time in dealing with the pensions received by men and their dependents with respect to service in the Korean war. I feel, however, in the light of our experience and the satisfaction with which the country has greeted efforts made on behalf of veterans in previous wars, that those who served in Korea will get at least as favourable consideration, if not better. The experience gained with respect to those who served in the previous wars will be invaluable in this regard.
I have not been able to deal in detail with the tremendous amount of work done by the war veterans allowance branch, but I find in the annual report that the recipients of war veterans allowances as at March 31, 1957 totalled 53,590. Here again I would like to pay tribute to the deputy ministers through the years, and particularly the former deputy minister, Walter Woods, for setting up an organization which has enabled all these matters to be dealt with in an expeditious and sympathetic way, and which has also enabled much of the red tape to be taken out of the administration of this department. This work has, I think, been very well carried on by the present deputy minister and the various heads of departments.
I have not done more than scratch the surface of this subject nor point out all the work done by the department, and I would apologize to those whose work I have not mentioned. I would commend to the members of this house a perusal of the annual report of the Department of Veterans Affairs so they may be made aware of the efforts of a very devoted department of our government.
I am sure the minister, having had long connection with the work for the veterans, the setting up of the veterans charter and the improvement of it from time to time, to which I know we are all devoted, has his heart in the making of this legislation as effective as it can be. I know he will want to see that it goes as far as it possibly can
Supply-Veterans Affairs to give expression to the feelings and desires of all our people to be fair to those who gave their services to their country in times of war. I extend to the minister and his associates in the department the very best of good wishes, and express the hope that the work which has been carried on so well up to now may be continued and improved in the years ahead.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak on the first item of these estimates I must again assure the minister of the support of this group for all his efforts on behalf of veterans, because we know that our cooperation in this respect will redound to the benefit of our comrades.
As a member of parliament I naturally take a very keen interest in the subject of veterans affairs, but I take a keen interest in it also for a number of other reasons. As one who was awarded the distinguished order of chattering teeth and quaking knees; as one whose father served in two world wars and at 82 kicked up a devil of a row because they would not take him as a quartermaster in the second world war; as one whose wife went to war with the old contemptibles as a nursing sister in 1914; as one who is the father of two daughters who served in the second war, and as the friend of many comrades in my own battalion and other battalions I have a deep, personal and abiding interest in this question.
Now, before proceeding with a few items of what I might describe as unfinished business, I want to express my appreciation of the work of the senior officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs including those delightful ladies, those charming senior officials who are so courteous and anxious to assist us and who, if they have not the information we seek, will usher us in the right direction to obtain the information. As the previous speaker said, I think this department sets an example for a good many other departments of government. This department is administered with every sympathy for the human beings those employed in it are trying to serve, and I feel that is generally recognized across the country.
I am going to make a sort of omnibus speech, Mr. Chairman, and I am going to save the time of the committee, as the previous speaker did, by taking the full time I have at my disposal.
I did not do that, though.

I am not going to deal with the Canadian Pension Act at this time, because Bill No. 38, to amend the act, will soon be before the house and we will have ample opportunity to bring its deficiencies to the attention of the minister when we discuss it.

Supply-Veterans Affairs However, I do want to deal with a number of matters. Some of them I have mentioned before, and I shall refer to them very briefly just to refresh the minister's memory so that when he gives consideration to amendments to veterans legislation he will have them all in order and in sequence.
With respect to the War Veterans' Allowance Act, I feel it should be amended to provide for certain unfortunate widows-and there are very few such cases-who are not married from the departmental point of view and who are not able to obtain the allowance because the husbands were not in receipt of the allowance before they died. I mentioned this on November 5, and my remarks will be found at pages 801 and 802 of Hansard of that date. I urge the minister to give some consideration to bringing in an amendment to correct that situation which will be of great benefit to those few people who suffer under the present terms of that section.
I want to bring to the minister's attention again the necessity for an amendment which would permit war veterans allowance recipients to leave Canada if their health required it, on the certificate of a departmental doctor *or medical officer. I am all for giving these war veterans allowance recipients the right to reside outside Canada for at least as long a time as that allowed the recipients of other welfare legislation. That is now possible. I do urge that consideration be given to this question. My previous reference to it can be found at page 801 of Hansard of November 5.
I also want to bring to the minister's attention the fact that there are quite a number of people in this country who think the veterans of the merchant navy have never received complete justice to date. They played a most vital role during the war, many of them suffering great hardship and danger, but they have been denied up to this time the benefits of the veterans charter. I urge that the minister consider an amendment to the War Veterans' Allowance Act that would bring them under this legislation.
I also think there is a necessity for an amendment to the act to provide for certain , dependent mothers not eligible at the present time. Here again these are rare cases where ' the veteran is the sole source of income for the mother concerned. I urge the minister to consider an amendment to the act to provide for those mothers who are at present destitute when their son, a war veterans allowance recipient, dies.
Naturally we support the constant Legion representations asking for an increase in the ceiling on permissive income to $1,200 for single persons and $2,000 for married persons. Those are the main things that require
attention so far as the War Veterans' Allowance Act is concerned. I hope when the minister replies he will indicate his attitude toward these suggestions for amendments which have come from the Canadian Legion and various parties in this house.
I wish now to deal with another matter that is of great importance to Canadian veterans and which is mentioned in the last brief presented to the cabinet by the Canadian Legion; that is, that the government give consideration to amendments to the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act. As far as I can ascertain this does not involve heavy expenditures, but it is a question of helping a number of children of war dead to secure a better education. In order to save the time of the committee and to be exact in presenting the case I am going to quote from the Legion brief, which says:
We have noted with some satisfaction the benefits which young people have derived from the above legislation in the last few years. We have also realized that the original act leaves out many children deserving of educational assistance. These groups, which we feel the provisions of the act should be extended to include, are:
(1)	Children entitled to receive pension because the father was in receipt of disability pension at the rate of 50 per cent or more at the time of death but whose death was not directly attributable to his service:
I know of a few cases that would be included if that amendment were provided. The Legion's request continued as follows:
(2)	Those children who are unable to pursue higher education as presently specified in the act and regulations but who take vocational and technical training to better fit them for employment.
I think there are more of those cases, but that does not necessarily mean any increase in expenditure. It does involve, however, a widening of the basis of the assistance, providing opportunities for boys and girls without academic qualifications but who want to learn trades and things of that sort; and if there is one thing we are short of in this country it is skilled tradesmen. Nearly every small community finds it difficult to secure people capable of doing electrical work, plumbing and carpentering and work of that nature. This provides an opportunity to correct that situation in the future by assisting those who would prefer to take technical and vocational rather than academic training. Because of the situation that exists at the present time the Canadian Legion recommends that the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act be amended to correct it.
I want to mention two amendments the Legion thinks are required in respect of the Veterans Insurance Act. This legislation has been of great benefit to veterans throughout
[Mr. Herridge.l

the years. First of all they ask for an extension of the application date for veterans insurance. The brief has this to say:
Unless a veteran of world war II still has reestablishment credit his opportunity to apply for veterans insurance was cut off on December 31, 1954, or 10 years after discharge, whichever was the later. Veterans of world war I were given 15 years, following cessation of hostilities, in which to avail themselves of similar protection.
I think that is a very reasonable request. I am one of those veterans who came back after the first world war concerned about re-establishing myself, regaining my health and things of that sort, and looking after a young brood of children. I did not realize for four or five years the advantages of this veterans insurance, but when I did realize it some years later I took out a policy because I was permitted to do so by the extension of the time limit. These veterans are growing older; they are accepting their responsibilities, and more and more they realize the advantages of this act. I do urge the minister to consider an amendment that would extend the date for application. The Legion brief bears out what I have to say in that connection, because it goes on to say:
Many disabled veterans seeking to provide security for their families, denied them by ordinary insurance, have found that their right to apply for veterans insurance has lapsed. There is no valid reason why the same privileges which were extended to world war I veterans cannot be made available to world war II veterans. The fact that this exists for those with re-establishment credits indicates its administrative acceptability.
As I said before, veterans more and more recognize the benefits they can obtain by taking out policies under this act, and I do urge the minister to repeat the procedure which was followed after the first world war. It is on this account that the Legion recommends:
That the government of Canada amend the Veterans Insurance Act to extend the date of application for world war II veterans to December 31, 1960. Comparable treatment should be accorded Korean veterans.
The Legion suggests a second amendment to the Veterans Insurance Act respecting disability pensions, section 10(1). It has this to say:
Widows of disability pensioners are deprived of the full effect as beneficiaries under the Veterans Insurance Act because they may receive less than the full death benefit of the policy. Technically, the veteran is charged with knowledge of this provision, but there is grave doubt that all understand its practical application. This is a violation of the accepted concept of life insurance.
The Legion therefore recommends:
That the government of Canada amend the Veterans Insurance Act to eliminate this section.
The minister will recall when we discussed this section of the Veterans Insurance Act. At that time he took exactly the same
Supply-Veterans Affairs stand we and other opposition members in the committee did. We took the stand taken by the Canadian Legion at that time, that the act should be amended to eliminate this discrimination. I ask the minister to give that his consideration.

I am still of the same
opinion I had then.

We are making these representations in this form because we know the minister is of the same opinion. We just want to back him up to the fullest extent.
I now want to say a word or two about the Veterans' Land Act administration, which has been very successful across this country. A good many veterans in my constituency settled under the provisions of this act, the greater number under the small holdings section of the act, but we also have a number settled on farms. I must say that in my conversations with veterans generally I find they much prefer to come under the jurisdiction, or the administration, of the Veterans' Land Act. It is for that reason that quite recently the national council of the Legion urged an amendment to bring part II of the Veterans' Land Act under the complete control of the Veterans' Land Act administration.
There is no question about it, the veteran does not like being transferred to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. They tell me in good numbers that under the present circumstances their application under part II is made through the Veterans' Land Act administration and is serviced in that way. Then when it comes to later administration, collection, advice, suggestion, and all that sort of thing, they are transferred to the jurisdiction of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. As a result of past experience, and because the departmental officials are sympathetic, they would very much prefer to remain under the Veterans' Land Act.
Mind you, when you read the figures in regard to collections under the Veterans' Land Act you find that the country does not suffer because of any deficiency in this respect. Because of the particular approach of the officials of this department and their knowledge of veterans problems, the veterans in Canada, generally speaking, would like under part II to come under the administration of the Veterans' Land Act. I would like to hear from the minister in this regard when he replies at the conclusion of this debate.
The Legion at a recent council meeting also asked for a reduction of the interest

Supply-Veterans Affairs rate to 3 per cent. In my opinion, and I think in the opinion of members of our group, the small holdings section of the Veterans' Land Act is one of the finest pieces of housing legislation we have in Canada, and we would like to see its principles extended to a much wider section of the population. We believe there is nothing better you can do to lay a sound foundation for good homes and well brought up families than by making provision for good housing.
I also want to make what I was going to say is my annual plea-it is now a perennial plea-for a reduction in the acreage required to qualify under the small holdings section of the Veterans' Land Act. Generally speaking it is ridiculous. If the land is valued at over $500 an acre, then it is 1.6 acres. I would admit that the officials of the Veterans' Land Act administration do everything possible to assist the veterans and make allowances for certain circumstances, and so on, within the terms of the law and the regulations.
As far as our district is concerned-and I know it applies to a good number of other districts in Canada-land for this purpose amounting to 1.6 acres, or three acres in larger areas, is not available because of the topography of the country. Right in my constituency there are still 200 veterans of whom I have knowledge who are being denied the opportunity to build under the small holdings section of the Veterans' Land Act, because they must get at least 1.6 acres which is valued at $500 an acre, or three acres if the land is of lesser value.
I do urge that consideration be given to reducing the acreage to the former half acre. In my district the majority of those men are working for the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, or are working in the mines, in the lumber mills or in the sawmills. I know from experience that if a veteran has a good home and half an acre of good land that is all he can look after. That half acre of good land is of great assistance in reducing the cost of living, particularly for the younger veteran raising a young family. I do urge consideration of a reduction in this acreage.
In conclusion I want to mention one other group which I think is being overlooked. I refer to the approximately 400 members of the Canadian overseas firefighter corps. We had this out in the veterans affairs committee years ago. The minister was very frank in expressing his opinion concerning these matters, along with a good number of others in this group. He was just as indignant as we were that they were not included in and given the benefits of the veterans charter legislation.
[Mr. Herridge.l
We all remember that When evidence was being given to the committee at the time on that particular point we were told, I think on very sound grounds, that these men were promised the benefits of the veterans charter and of the veterans legislation prior to leaving for Canada. At this time there are only approximately 400 of them in Canada. You will find them scattered all over the country. A few of them are serving in various fire brigades.
I do urge that consideration be given to the very reasonable case that has been advanced for the consideration of these men under the legislation provided for veterans in this country.
Those are the particular pieces of unfinished business that I wanted to bring to the attention of the minister and the committee. I will have a few things to say about hospital administration, admissions and things of that sort, and there are also a few other matters I wish to raise, but I will bring those up under the appropriate items.
Finally may I say there is no question that throughout the years there has been a continual improvement in veterans legislation, and we must give great credit to the major veterans organizations, the Canadian Legion and the national council of veterans, for that improvement. Those organizations have constantly paid attention to the needs of veterans and the legislation required to meet those needs. They have brought them to the attention of members of parliament and the veterans affairs committee when they had the opportunity, and have informed us very fully from time to time.
We recognize that we have some of the finest veterans legislation in the world, but I trust the government will give favourable consideration to the suggestions for amendments to remedy certain deficiencies in our legislation which will be brought to the attention of the minister by various members in this debate. We have done so well up to now, and the cost of what we may have to do in the future is very small in relation to the total cost at the present time. We can achieve so much with so little. I am not going to go further into what we should do, because the hon. member for Selkirk will be our second speaker on item 1 and I am going to leave him to deal with that question.

Mr. Chairman, at the outset of my remarks I want to assure the minister that he will at all times receive the sincere co-operation of the members of this group in his endeavours to improve veterans legislation. I think we are fortunate in having

very fine personnel in the Department of Veterans Affairs but, of course, they can only go as far as the legislation permits them. I also find that when I hear criticisms of the Department of Veterans Affairs they should in reality be criticisms of certain pieces of legislation they have to administer, and I am sure the minister will endeavour to bring down legislation from time to time to improve the operation of the department.
I think the minister has done very well so far. He has brought down amendments to the War Veterans' Allowance Act which have been a substantial improvement. We also have amendments to the Pension Act. I think those amendments should go considerably farther, and I will have something to say on that later.
On November 6 the minister stated that it was his intention to set up a veterans affairs committee at the next session of parliament with power to review all veterans legislation. That is a most pleasant departure from the past practice whereby the veterans affairs committee has been tied down to very narrow terms of reference. We have just been allowed to consider the specific piece of legislation referred to the committee.
I am hoping that when the minister decides to set up the committee on veterans affairs he will set it up as a standing committee. There has been a demand from veterans organizations and members of the house for a number of years that the veterans affairs committee be a standing committee. It would not involve any increase in cost to the government, and it does seem to me that is one of the recommendations of the veterans organizations the minister could very well carry out.
I want to turn now to the Pension Act. The hon. member for Kootenay West stated that we would have an opportunity to discuss the Pension Act when the bill was before us, but the bill has a number of specific amendments in it and as the matters I want to bring up are outside those amendments it would not, strictly speaking, be in order to bring them up when we are discussing the bill on pensions.
Let me make it clear that the criticism I have to make is not in any way a criticism of the pension commission; for, as I have already said, they are tied down by the legislation, and I think certain changes are necessary in order that a wider interpretation may be given in certain matters regarding pensions.
