Mr. Chairman, the sections of the Pension Act to which I wish to refer are sections 13 and 70. Section 70 used to be section 62. There has been a great deal of discussion concerning these two sections in former veterans affairs committees. The minister and his colleague the Minister of Public Works have been quite eloquent in their pleas to get amendment to these two sections.
Section 13 deals with disabilities of preenlistment origin. We in this group have always taken the stand that a veteran's condition as recorded on his medical sheet at the time of enlistment should be regarded as his true condition, and that no attempt should be made to refuse a pension on the ground that the disability arose from a condition recorded some time prior to enlistment. We might have a case where a veteran was in hospital five or six years before he enlisted, and he was discharged as being cured. Later, when that record is looked up, the stand is taken that the condition for which he is seeking a pension actually arose out of the condition he had at the time he was in hospital and for which he was discharged as being cured.
The Legion has taken a similar stand. I notice that in the brief they presented to the cabinet last fall they recommended that section 13 (1) (a) of the Pension Act be amended so that where a pension applicant who has served in an actual theatre of war is found to have a disability resulting from injury or disease not recorded on his medical examination prior to enlistment, such injury or disease shall be presumed to have incurred or had its inception subsequent to enlistment. All I am going to say is that I hope the minister will give very careful consideration to that section, to see whether or not it might be possible to get a little closer to that principle.
I have often heard people criticize the pension commission for the decisions that they bring down in relation to that section. I would say that in the vast majority of cases it was not the pension commission that were to blame but it was the wording of the section. I do not believe we can hope to have any improvement in that matter unless we have an amendment to section 13 along the lines suggested by the Canadian Legion.
The other section, section 70, is I think far more important. You may say that it is the veteran's last resort in so far as getting a pension is concerned. There has been a lot of discussion about this section in the

Supply-Veterans Affairs veterans committee. I recall that in 1948, I think it was, the late member for Lanark, Dr. Blair, moved an amendment in order to try to get a wider interpretation of the benefit of doubt. His amendment was to strike out the words "is entitled to draw"

perhaps I had better read section 70:
Notwithstanding anything in this act, on any application for pension the applicant is entitled to the benefit of the doubt, which means that it is not necessary for him to adduce conclusive proof of his right to the pension applied for. but the body adjudicating on the claim-
Here, I should like to interject that the words used to be "is entitled to draw". Those are the words which the hon. member moved to strike out in committee.
-shall draw from all the circumstances of the case, the evidence adduced and medical opinions, all reasonable inferences and presumptions in favour of the applicant.
The hon. member moved that the words as I say, "is entitled to draw", be struck out. I was very sceptical as to whether or not that would make any difference because the words "shall draw" were in the act before and I could not see how the words "is entitled to draw" could affect the words "shall draw". However, the committee felt that it might be an improvement so the committee voted to strike out the words. The minister expressed approval of that amendment. I still claim section 70 is not wide enough. I am not quarrelling with the interpretation of the pension commission. I claim you will never get satisfaction from section 70 until the pension commission are given wider discretionary powers. The trouble is the pension commission have not the discretionary powers necessary to give a soldier a fair deal.
I am going to cite one case. I do not like citing cases, but in view of the fact this case has received a great deal of publicity through the Veterans' Advocate of November issue, I think it is well to read it. The minister can then say whether or not the explanation in the Veterans' Advocate is fair. Let me read it:
Another matter which needs urgent attention is a confirmation of the obligation to give the veteran always the benefit of the element of doubt. Especially in the case of death by cancer. As we write we have before us the history of a Winnipeg veteran whose widow and children have recently been denied a pension. This man suffered gunshot wounds in his back during world war II. He was discharged with a 30 per cent disability. As the years passed his back began to bother him. After many medical examinations it was finally discovered that a soft-nosed bullet still was embedded near his spine. This was finally removed in 1949. His condition continued to deteriorate until he died in 1956 from cancer, which the autopsy report stated was very widespread. There was no positive proof that this disease was caused by gunshot wounds, but there also is no positive proof that


it was not. There definitely was proof of negligence inasmuch as the bullet in question was not discovered for several years. We realize that should this widow be granted a pension it might pave the way for many other claims. However, we contend that the element of doubt is there and that a pension should be awarded and that the act should be changed to strengthen claims where such doubt is present.
As I say, I do not know whether or not that is a fair description of the case, but if that is a true description then I believe the majority of the members of the house would agree that the widow should receive a pension. It may be that the doctors were of the definite opinion that that man died from cancer, and that his condition had not been affected by the bullet being embedded in the back near the spine for six years, but as I understand it the medical profession is not too certain as to the actual cause of cancer. Is the medical profession in a position to say that the fact the bullet had been embedded in the back for six years could not have had some effect upon that veteran's condition? I doubt it.
But even so, and granting that the medical doctors of the commission were justified in ruling that there was no doubt in this case that the man had died from cancer and the fact he had had a bullet in his back had nothing to do with that cancer, nevertheless I say in the light of all the facts of this case as disclosed in this article, the widow should receive a pension because for six years that man had a bullet in his back and his condition was deteriorating. Surely, the very least we could do as a form of compensation would be to award the widow a pension today. I say, therefore, what we need today is an amendment to section 70 to give the pension commission wider discretion. I am sure if the commission had it in their power to give the widow a pension, they would do so but they feel, under the terms of the section they are not able to do so. I say let us amend section 70 in such a way as to give the pension commission a greater discretion in such matters.
I now want to turn to the Veterans' Land Act. I have been somewhat concerned over the number of veterans who have been settled under the act and who are leaving the land. These veterans are not by any means misfits. They are not men who have failed. I would say that in the majority of cases the veterans who are leaving the land are men who are highly efficient and ambitious but who are not prepared to see their families continue to be obliged to live under the present low standard of living when they know very well that if they leave the farms and go into the cities they can greatly improve their condition.

I have followed a number of these cases through where men who were having a hard struggle on the farms left the farms and went into the city. I find that in the majority of cases those men have done extremely well. In my opinion a person is making a big mistake when he thinks that when a veteran or any other man leaves the farm today it is because he is inefficient or a misfit. That is not the reason. The reason is that they are ambitious, especially for their families. The other day somebody told me, "A man must have a love for the soil to carry on on the farm". I say that a man must have a greater love. His first love should be for his family. If that man knows that by continuing on the farm he is not going to be able to give his family the standard of living they deserve, his love for the soil will have to take second place to his love for his family.
I therefore think the officials of the Veterans' Land Act should do everything they can to help veterans to make the necessary financial arrangements to pay off their land and to leave the farm if they so desire because I do not believe you can ever hope for a soldier settler to be successful on the land once he desires to leave it, once he is no longer satisfied, or once his family is no longer satisfied.
I am suggesting that the officials should not try to stop him from leaving. We have now reached the stage where many veterans are now able to get clear title to their equipment and their livestock and many of them are able to make some financial arrangements whereby the amount remaining owing on the farm can be paid off. In some cases they assign their pension. In other cases they will assign the amount they receive from the farm to the Veterans' Land Act administration. Where satisfactory arrangements of that kind can be made, where a settler is desirous to leave the farm I think it would be a great mistake for the officials to try to put anything in the way of his leaving the farm.
After all, it must be remembered that most of the veterans who settled under the Veterans' Land Act had limited capital. In many cases their operations today are not large enough to give them the type of standard of living which they would be able to obtain if they went into another walk of life. Mind you, I am not criticizing the Veterans' Land Act. I think it is a good act. Unfortunately the situation that exists is that agriculture today is a distressed industry. Whether a man be a returned man or a civilian, if he is on the farm today in the majority of cases he is having a struggle to 96698-107J
Supply-Veterans Affairs keep his head above water and at the same time maintain a standard of living that he deserves.
I want to say a few words with regard to the soldiers who settled under the old soldiers settlement act. It will be remembered that for a number of years the late member for Battle River, Mr. Robert Fair, used to introduce a motion to give clear title to veterans who had settled under the old soldiers settlement board. He received a very sympathetic hearing from the members of this house but no action was taken to give them a clear title, although I think we must agree that the government was quite considerate in cutting down the amount owing by those veterans. After all, the purpose of the soldiers settlement act was to try to re-establish these veterans within a period of 25 years. We find that 50 per cent of those veterans failed to become established. Today, 38 years after the veterans were settled under that act, we find there are still 39 veterans accounts unsettled, with an average debt of $616. I suggest to the minister that we could very well, at this late date, wipe out those accounts entirely. These veterans are getting old. They have not many years to live. They would like to have a clear title to their land. I think the least we could do now is to say to them, "We realize that you have had a struggle; you have stayed on the land and we are going to wipe out what you owe".
The other matter to which I should like to refer is the merchant seamen. As I understand it, today the only merchant seamen who can come under the Veterans' Land Act are those merchant seamen who are in receipt of a pension. I want to refresh the minister's memory with regard to the attitude taken by the veterans' affairs committee in the past during the war in connection with the merchant seamen. I have here a copy of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the special committee on land settlement of veterans of the present war for the sitting on June 23, 1942. We had Mr. Arthur Randles, director of merchant seamen, Department of Transport, before us. This is what he said:
-it is recommended that Canadian merchant seamen be permitted to participate under the land settlement arrangements, provided that their record shows they have served for an appreciable period in dangerous waters or zones during the present hostilities, and I would suggest that a period of three months' service might be taken as a guide to determine their eligibility to participate. This is in line with the general requirements for the issuance of a merchant navy badge. In any case, under circumstances where a Canadian merchant navy badge is not issued, evidence of service in hazardous zones can be provided by the seamen's discharge documents.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
I just want to quote what the minister of veterans affairs at that time had to say with regard to this question. Hon. Ian Mackenzie stated as follows:
My own opinion is that the men of the merchant navy are entitled to any and all of the privileges which anybody else serving in this war overseas or elsewhere gets. As I see it, they are twice as much in the line of fire.
The committee discussed that matter at some length. Later the minister said he thought it would be a mistake to allow the merchant seamen immediately after the war to be eligible to settle under the Veterans' Land Act because he said these men are needed on the sea. But he said at a later date that we might be able to change our decision in that regard. I would ask you to mark well the report that was made with regard to that matter and dated July 7, 1942:
That at a later date this act-
That is the Veterans' Land Act.
-be so amended as to make provision for persons having had service on ships, who are not in receipt of a disability pension.
I do not think anybody can argue today that we should not allow merchant seamen to come under the Veterans' Land Act for the reason that they are needed on the sea. Today we seem to have a number of surplus seamen, especially when we transfer Canadian ships to foreign registry. I think the minister might give that matter consideration and see whether or not it would be possible to make merchant seamen who had service in a danger zone eligible to come under the Veterans' Land Act. I am not suggesting that they should come in as full time farmers, but it would be of tremendous help to these men if they could take advantage of the small holding section of the act and perhaps have a small holding alongside the sea coast and possibly continue with a certain amount of fishing.
I see that my time is nearly up. I hope the minister will also give that matter his careful consideration so that at the next session when the veterans affairs committee meets he may be in a position to recommend some action be taken in that regard.
The only other matter to which I want to refer now-and it is one that I do not think I could raise on any other section-is the question of the aged veteran. I want to commend the Department of Veterans Affairs for their sympathetic attitude toward the aged veteran. I have received from veterans a number of applications or requests to try to find jobs for them. They have said, "We do not want to have to apply for the war veterans allowance; we would like to get

some work. Could you get us a job perhaps with some department?" I have taken the matter up with the Department of . Veterans Affairs. They have sent a counsellor over to interview the man and in the majority of cases they have found ways and means by which that man could be employed. In some cases they have recommended that he make application to the corps of commissionaires. I think it is called the Canadian corps of commissionaires.
In that way they have been able to get employment. There is one thing I would like to ask the minister to explain. I have looked at the report of the Department of Veterans Affairs and there is a reference to this corps; it states it does not receive any subsidy from the government. I wonder if the minister would explain how this corps is financed; how many offices it has across the dominion, and what connection, if any, there is between the Canadian corps of commissionaires and the Department of Veterans Affairs.

In rising to speak for the first time in this house, Mr. Chairman, I would first like to pay a tribute to the hon. minister who heads the department and whose estimates we are now considering. The hon. minister is spokesman for the province in which we are now living, but he is also a veteran of distinguished service to his country, firstly as an officer in the New Brunswick fighting 26th battalion during world war I; secondly, he has rendered continuous service between the wars in the militia of this country; thirdly, he served throughout the whole of world war II, and now lastly on account of his record as a member of parliament for 22 years. During this period he has been almost continuously a member of the veterans affairs committee. His record is there and it speaks for itself.
It has been said that the Canadian veterans legislation is the best in the world. I think we all agree with that, Mr. Chairman, and it is a tribute to all of those who have served in the previous parliaments of this country.
Hear, hear.

In my opinion it is also a great tribute to those who have served in another organization the name of which I have heard mentioned very often in our deliberations on the War Veterans' Allowance Act. The name of the organization to which I refer, of course, is the Canadian Legion which, for the past 30 years, has played such a vital part in guiding, advising and helping the government in its decisions with respect to veterans legislation. Like many who returned from this last war-and for that matter from the first world war-and being

grateful that I had been spared to come home to my family, I determined that I would try to help those with whom I had served and their dependents. In the Canadian Legion I found the vehicle through which I could work. That organization has given outstanding help to the veterans and in the past score of years the leadership which it has attracted on its top level has been invaluable; I refer to such men as Alex Walker, Basil Price, Lionel Baxter, Alf Watts and Dr. Lumsden. Alex Walker, indeed, spent the full five years of the war here in Ottawa so that he could be near to the government and assist them in their decisions concerning war veterans' welfare. Dr. John Anderson is another man whose name I should mention and now David Burgess. All these men have given service of the highest calibre. The Legion is a big organization of more than a quarter of a million men and women. It is unfortunate that all the veterans of this country do not belong to the organization in order to give it even greater strength but we must not, of course, minimize the fact that there are other veterans' organizations. However, the Canadian Legion is the spokesman and has been the spokesman for the veterans.
In my own work as provincial president for that organization and also as a member of the dominion council I had the opportunity on two occasions to appear before members of the previous government, the government which was headed by the right hon. gentleman who is now the Leader of the Opposition. I would like to say that when we appeared with our briefs no group could have been received more kindly or more courteously. The representations of any group could not have been listened to with more attention than the representations made by the Legion on behalf of the veterans. I just wanted to pay that tribute to the right hon. gentleman and to his former colleagues.
That the work of the Department of Veterans Affairs was of considerable standing and would be projected far into the future was brought home to me very forcibly not very long ago when I read that recently the last pension attributable to the war of 1812 had just been paid in the United States. It seems rather amazing that it would last that long, that there would still be someone who was pensionable from that war. It therefore is likely that the task of the Department of Veterans Affairs will go beyond the time of any of us here today, even taking into account the hope, which I am sure is shared by all of us, that we will never have another war.
I recently had an opportunity to converse with the senior officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs, along with other members of the department, many of whom are
Supply-Veterans Affairs here today with the minister. I was amazed at the scope of the work they are now doing. When we realize there are 190,000 active pension cases coming under the Canadian pension commission, that the war veterans allowance department has over 57,000 active cases; that the Veterans' Land Act deals with over 58,000 cases and that there are over 10,000 men and women in our hospitals under active treatment, we realize the tremendous scope of the work of this department.
I do not wish to take too long because I realize this house wishes to get on with the estimates and not to be held up, but I would like to speak about two or three things in connection with veterans legislation. To my mind, one of the finest acts that was ever passed in this house was that passed in 1953, namely the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act. I say this because that act provided for the children of those men who had given their lives in world war II or who had since died from their wounds. There is, however, one regrettable feature in this respect, in that it took eight years from the end of the war before the act was passed and undoubtedly many youngsters during that period did not have the benefit of this legislation. I particularly recall a case in the city in which I live, the city of Fredericton, where a man who had served as a sergeant in world war I and in world war II was back in the forces because he was determined to be there. He served as a major in the regiment in which I also served and gave his life on D-day on the shores of France. He should not have been there, of course, and they did everything to keep him from going, but he was determined to lead his company on the shores that day and he was killed.
Now this man left two children and by 1953 the children had already received their education with the help of their widowed mother and also with some help from the Legion, from scholarships and bursaries. As I say, it is regrettable that we cannot undo the past; it is regrettable the act was not implemented at the end of the war.
I would like to speak for a moment about the benevolent funds. The story of the canteen fund of the first world war is not a happy one and perhaps through mismanagement or lack of wisdom the fund was rapidly depleted in many provinces. Those who emerged safely from the last war when the funds of the canteens and messes were frozen had the benefit of that experience and the benevolent funds of the army, navy and air force were set up. It seems to me they have been most wisely administered. I can speak from personal experience especially about the army benevolent fund.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
I can well remember at the dominion conference of the Legion in 1946 sitting on a committee that considered very seriously how this fund would be administered. The present deputy minister if I remember correctly was a member of that committee. Over the years the fund which at that time, if I am not mistaken, was something like $7 million has been most wisely administered and has served an extremely useful purpose.
The hon. member who spoke just before I rose referred to the corps of commissionaires and addressed several questions to the minister. I would not attempt to speak for the minister but since I wanted to discuss this question too my remarks may be of assistance with respect to one or two of the problems raised because I have been deeply interested in the corps of commissionaires.
The corps of commissionaires is administered by a board of governors, in the case of our own province a board consisting of 40 men who serve without remuneration of any kind and are the guiding body for the corps. In the case of our province perhaps the most distinguished member is the lieutenant governor of New Brunswick, himself a war amputee as a result of service in the first world war and a man keenly interested in the welfare of his comrades and their dependents. The corps is non-political, nonpartisan and non-profitmaking. It has no connection in that manner with any other organization. The governors arrange employment for the members of the corps. They are suitably uniformed and it seems to me that only the highest calibre of man is attracted to this corps.
I know of a very fine man in my own community who served initially in the Boer war and then in world war I and finally in world war II. The amazing thing is that he was granted his commission in world war II. I do not know just how old he is but it does not matter because he is still a young looking and active gentleman. I believe there is no finer example of a serving commissionaire.
Perhaps I neglected to say that five cents per hour is deducted from the fee which industry pays to the board of governors for the services of the men in the corps and that money is used for administration purposes, uniforms and certain other things. This splendid oragnization provides those men who do not wish to accept charity an opportunity of working and earning a decent living. The government of this country spends many millions of dollars annually in the interests of the Canadian people but I submit there is no group in this great country that is more worthy of consideration than

those who served and the dependents of those who served when Canada was engaged in the terrible conflicts of this century.
It is and has always been a source of great satisfaction to me to be able to express words of commendation to the Department of Veterans Affairs and as a veteran I can say to this department-and as Canadians we all can say this-"Well done, good and faithful servants."

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take this opportunity of expressing my general support of the recommendations contained in the brief recently submitted to the government of Canada by the dominion command of the Canadian Legion. I should like in particular to express my unqualified support of their recommendation with respect to Newfoundland veterans which reads as follows:
The Canadian Legion therefore recommends that a change be made in the Pension Act to make clear the status of these Newfoundland veterans in accordance with the spirit of the negotiations leading up to the terms of union and with the intent of the legislators as reflected in the other legislation quoted above.
I was very pleased to find that the brief dealt with the special problem of Newfoundland veterans at some length as found at pages 10, 11 and 12 of their submission. I do not intend to repeat the arguments to be found here which are almost indentical with the statements I made in the house as reported at page 914 of Hansard of November 8. However, I believe it would be useful and convenient, not only to hon. members of this committee but to those of the public who read Hansard if I were to place on the record the relevant sections of the legislation referred to in the Legion brief. The relevant section of the Canadian Pension Act is section 13, subsections 5, 6 and 7 which read as follows:
Section 13-
(5)	For the purposes of sections 50, 51 and 52, domicile in Newfoundland shall be deemed to be domicile in Canada.
(6)	A member of the naval or military forces of Newfoundland in world war I or world war II shall be deemed to be a member of the forces for the purposes of this section.
(7)	A British subject resident and domiciled in Newfoundland at the time of enlistment who served in the naval, army or air forces of His Majesty or in any of the naval, army or air forces of any of the countries allied with His Majesty during world war II shall be deemed to be a member of the forces for the purposes of this section, if the disability in respect of which the application is made is not pensionable by virtue of subsection (5) or (6).
The Canadian pension commission has interpreted these sections to mean that Newfoundland veterans are no different from Canadians who left Canada to enlist in the

Imperial services and therefore they cannot be treated as if they had served in Her Majesty's Canadian forces as stated in the opening paragraph of the terms of union on which it was intended the status of Newfoundland veterans under confederation would be based.
Hon. members will recall that the opening section in the terms of union relating to veterans stated that Newfoundland veterans would be treated on the same basis as if they had served in the Canadian forces. In contrast, when we examine other legislation we find that this interpretation is expressly written into the act. For example the relevant section of the War Veterans' Allowance Act is section 30, subsection 11 (a) which reads as follows:
-for the purposes of this act,
(a)	the expression "Canadian forces" includes any forces raised in Newfoundland and "domicile in Canada" and "residence in Canada" include respectively domicile and residence in Newfoundland, whether before or after the union of Newfoundland with Canada.
The Veterans Rehabilitation Act is even more explicit. The relative section of this act is section 6 (1) which reads as follows:
For the purposes of sections 7, 8, 9 and 11, a Newfoundland veteran who has been discharged shall be deemed to be a veteran as defined in section 2.
Section 2 reads as follows:
In this section the expression "Newfoundland veteran" means a person who served on active service.
(a)	in any of the naval or army forces of Newfoundland or having been recruited in Newfoundland in any of the naval, army or air forces raised in Newfoundland by or on behalf of the United Kingdom; or
(b)	in any other naval, army or air forces of His Majesty and at the time of his enlistment therein was domiciled in Newfoundland; or
(c)	In any of the naval, army or air forces of the nations allied with His Majesty in active operations against the enemy in world war II, if he was domiciled in Newfoundland at the time of his enlistment therein and was domiciled and resident in Newfoundland within two years from the date of his discharge therefrom or the 8th day of May, 1945, whichever is the later.
It will be seen that the status of the Newfoundland veteran is very clear in the definitions set forth in the Veterans Rehabilitation Act and in the War Veterans' Allowance Act, but when it comes to the Canadian Pension Act there is some ambiguity. I should like to join with the hon. member for Acadia in urging that either the Canadian pensions commission be given greater discretionary powers or that the relative sections be amended to clarify the Pension Act to bring it into line with the other two acts and in line also with the intentions of the legislators, as set forth in the terms of union.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
At this time I should also like to support the recommendations of the Canadian Legion with respect to the merchant navy. I have already referred to this group, as can be found in Hansard of November 6 at page 823. Hon. members will have received a further brief from the Canadian merchant navy veterans association, and I should like to join with the other members who have supported the requests contained in this brief.
The basis on which a war veterans allowance is paid is the theory that a veteran who served in His Majesty's forces is burnt out by reason of his services in comparison with those who did not serve. I am sure that this theory can be with equal validity applied to the merchant navy as to any other of the three services. These people suffered severe casualties, as I pointed out before. In some settlements in my district the casualties in the merchant navy, the numbers actually killed, were far in excess of those of any of the other services, and in some instances even in excess of the three services together. These merchant navy veterans underwent all the hazards of war, including gunfire, aerial bombing and torpedoing and, as a result of their misfortunes they often had to suffer the hardships of being left in the sea for hours on end, floating around in cold water, in shark-infested waters, or drifting for days in the ocean in very small boats.
I am sure everyone will agree that hardships of this kind must tend to shorten a man's life and make him age much more rapidly than would normally be the case. I strongly recommend that the minister consider the claims set forth in the brief of the Canadian merchant navy veterans association that the burnt-out pension be extended to veterans of the merchant navy.
I agree with the hon. member for Acadia that there is no good reason now why the merchant navy veterans should not have some of the benefits of the Veterans' Land Act and also civil service preference. I strongly recommend this to the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I know that he cannot do a great deal at this moment, but very soon he will be considering his departmental estimates for the coming year, and I do hope he will be able to bring down at the next session the necessary changes in veterans welfare legislation to implement the recommendations of this brief and that he will find it possible to include the necessary provisions in his subsequent estimates.

My colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay West, dealt with a great many of the problems the veteran has today and I am not going to touch on these. It seems to me that when we begin to talk about veterans affairs the chips drop off everybody's
