Supply-Veterans Affairs shoulders and everybody is ready to agree with the other fellow because it is something that is really needed.
The hon. member for Kootenay West dealt with some of the amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act. The first one was to benefit certain married women. The second one had to do with residence outside Canada. The third one dealt with certain dependent mothers, and then there was the increase in the ceiling up to $1,200 for single veterans and $2,000 for married veterans. Then, there was the inclusion of the veterans of the merchant navy. He talked about educational assistance, amendments to the Veterans Insurance Act and to the Veterans' Land Act, improved hospital treatment regulations and many minor adjustments. Therefore, I would be taking up a lot of the time unnecessarily if I repeated these things, because I believe in the thoughts that he expressed when he was speaking on this matter.
There is one thing that I do want to ask the minister about and that is this. When a veteran becomes mentally ill and is taken to a hospital and remains there for some considerable time does he get his pension while he is there, or what part of it does he get? Should the veteran get better, does he get what is coming to him when he leaves the hospital? If he dies, does the remainder that is left at the hospital revert to the crown?
I should like answers to these questions because I want to relay the answers to other veterans in Manitoba. I support the hon. member for Acadia in bringing up the soldier settlement problem. I think he said there are only 39 left now. We who farmed through the bad years must realize the hell they went through trying to keep body and soul together. I have a lot of these farms in my constituency and it must have been known from the time these men went on the land that it would never be possible for them to make good. They have not got clear titles yet, and if there are only 39 left I appeal most sincerely to the minister to give them a clear title because they deserve it.
There is another matter that has been brought up repeatedly in past years. I refer to the firefighters. I know that the minister is familiar with the matter because he has been here longer than I have. I feel quite sure he knows the story, that General Lafleche said they would be taken care of, but very little has been done for them. I think that they should get some consideration. I have a letter here from the president of the firefighters association in which he says:
Our overseas firefighters in Winnipeg number 25 and we are in constant touch with members in the other provinces and no doubt you may hear from their respective members of parliament in our favour . . .


That is the other matter I wanted to bring up and I ask the minister to give it some reconsideration. I have also had some correspondence with the minister about some people who wrote me concerning Deer Lodge hospital. The gentleman I spoke to last about it wanted to know if the government was getting so hard up that it had to collect $500 a ward to establish wards. The minister was good enough to take up the matter. However, we have never got to the bottom of it and I should like to get to the bottom of it. Moneys are voted here in parliament for Deer Lodge hospital and why the hospital should need to ask organizations for donations merely so that the organization can have its name given to the ward I do not know. The minister can tell me about that when he is answering all the questions.
The Department of Veterans Affairs is one of the largest departments of the government and is asking for a budget of approximately $250 million this year. I brought in a resolution last year seeking the establishment of a permanent committee on veterans affairs. It was only before the house for one day and 19 members spoke in the debate, 20 including myself. Only two were against the resolution. Everybody else was in favour of it. I think such a committee is just as much needed this year as it was last year.
The argument has always been put up that a special committee of the house can be set up any time it is needed. I have now sat in the house under four ministers of veterans affairs, the late Hon. Ian Mackenzie, the Hon. Milton Gregg, the Hon. Hugues Lapointe and now the present minister. These hon. gentlemen could be classed as professional soldiers who knew as much as any other veteran knew.
Veterans affairs are going to continue to be with us, but the type of man who will head the department will change over the years and that is the reason I am so anxious to see a permanent committee on veterans affairs set up. Some day in the near future the head of the department will be a civil servant but not necessarily a veteran. A minister who has never seen active service can never be expected to understand the problems of the veteran in the same way as one who has had that experience.
May I say here, to make sure that I am understood, that I have nothing whatever against the people holding the various jobs in the department today. Over the years I have been here I have got to know them personally. They have become intimate friends of mine and I have repeatedly gone to them for advice in cases that have been brought to my attention. But the men who are

there today are going to come to the end of the road soon and we are not going to have veterans in these positions. The sooner we get it in black and white that we will have a committee every year the better it will be for everybody.
Our veterans, including those of world war I and world war II, constitute a significant proportion of the total Canadian population. We have only to remind ourselves that 66,651 lost their lives in the first world war and 44,891 in the second world war. Furthermore, such a committee would facilitate the presentation of veterans problems by the Canadian Legion and other recognized organizations in Canada. Often in the past there have been times when there has been no committee on veterans affairs with the result that important problems affecting veterans and their families did not receive the proper airing to which they were entitled.
The Department of Veterans Affairs acts in an administrative capacity in dealing with veterans problems. Competent as the department may be in this role, the fact is that our veterans require additional attention which is beyond the scope of the administrators in the department. If a permanent committee were established and if it sat every session it was required parliament would be in a much better position to determine when changes in veterans legislation were required.
I feel sure that a veterans affairs committee dealing with these matters from year to year would be able to see that the legislation passed for the benefit of veterans was maintained and used for the benefit of veterans. Only by having a permanent veterans affairs committee of the house, which can keep close to the needs of the veteran, are we going to get the kind of administration the veterans should have.
I am pleased to learn from the minister that he is going to set up a permanent veterans affairs committee at the next session of parliament. I want to congratulate the minister on making this decision. I may say to the minister that my resolution is on the order paper and when it comes up for discussion I will let it stand and drop it to the bottom of the list. The minister will make many veterans happy across this broad dominion. The Legion asked for a permanent veterans affairs committee and I have their request here. When the Minister of Public Works spoke last spring he quoted the resolution passed by the Legion at their convention in Vancouver in June, 1956. As found at page 951 of Hansard for Feburary 4, 1957, it is in these words:
Whereas the government has not seen fit to appoint a committee on veterans affairs during the present session of parliament:
Supply-Veterans Affairs
Whereas problems are continually arising concerning the Pension Act, War Veterans' Allowance Act, et cetera:
Be it resolved that this convention make representations for the appointment of a permanent standing committee on veterans affairs to which all such problems would be referred.
I am sure that everyone is going to congratulate the minister for making such a bold move. I know that when he was on this side of the house he gave full support to such legislation as we tried to get passed. It has been an uphill fight to try to get that but I do not for one minute think the minister will go back on me now. He told me he would do this, and I am withdrawing my resolution knowing full well that the minister will keep his word.

I should like to be associated with those who spoke so kindly of the work of the department and with respect to the operations of the department itself. Certainly the spirit of co-operation we have had has been excellent. I may say that the Legion members in my area are very appreciative of it. I think the veterans are extremely fortunate to have a minister sympathetic to their cause. Those of us who have been on the special committee on veterans affairs and in the house in former years recall so well how frequently he spoke on behalf of the veterans. I am satisfied that if it is at all possible to have certain legislation introduced that would assist the veterans even more, he will do his level best to attain that end.
I speak at this time to give my measure of support to any legislation the minister may propose so that any influence we might have may result in such legislation finally being brought about. The hon. member for Selkirk just mentioned the resolution he had calling for a standing committee on veterans affairs. I hope the minister will be able to carry out his desire and introduce legislation next year to bring about such a committee. Last year when the hon. member for Selkirk introduced his resolution I was one who spoke in favour of it. I certainly have not changed my mind in the meantime. I was very pleased the other day when the minister, in speaking on veterans affairs, indicated that he, too, was going along with the idea.
There are two particular matters about which I want to speak today. One of these matters was touched upon only slightly when we had the bill on war veterans' allowance before us. I refer to the submission in the Canadian Legion brief respecting merchant seamen. At that time I indicated to the house that I could not recall the merchant seamen being represented before the committee, but apparently on June 7 and 8, 1954 a representative of these seamen was before

Supply-Veterans Affairs the committee. He drew their problem to our attention. The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo has spoken on this question on more than one occasion, and I would certainly concur with him and with the hon. member for Acadia and others who have spoken on behalf of the merchant seamen. I feel that their case is deserving of every consideration.
I find I am not alone in my thinking. The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo had a brief from these merchant seamen and I do not know whether or not he has the same information I have but certainly some of us received a copy of the brief. I do have a facsimile of a letter signed by J. G. Diefen-baker. This letter was written on March 2, 1948 and it is addressed to A. J. Heide, secretary-treasurer, Canadian Merchant Na' Veterans' Association, Montreal. It reads:
Dear Mr. Heide,
I thank you and your association for your letter of February 24th.
I will bring the case of you veterans to the attention of the house when the veterans committee is set up.
Those that won the "Battle of the Atlantic" deserve to receive the same treatment as other veterans of our country.
Again thanking you for your letter, I am,
Yours sincerely,
J. G. Diefenbaker.
I realize that the Prime Minister was then a private member of the house, but I feel sure he has not changed his sentiments, at least, I hope he has not. If he felt the merchant seamen were deserving at that time of being included in and given the same rights and status as veterans, then I think their case is just as commendable today and possibly even more so when we see so many of these merchant seamen in the difficulties in which they are today. I find, sir, that this question of assistance for merchant seamen is not a thought that was just brought hastily to the attention of this house at this time, nor is it something about which former governments were not made aware. I have information that the Hon. Brooke Claxton, who was minister of national defence in 1951, received representations from this same association asking for inclusion of merchant seamen in the veterans' legislation. Later Hugues Lapointe, who is not with us now, received such a request. In fact, he gave some recognition to it by introducing the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act, under which the children of merchant seamen were eligible for assistance. Then, the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount, who was minister of transport at the time, came to Vancouver last year and was met by representatives of the seamen's union. They approached him with the same plea. It seems that cabinet


ministers were quite approachable, but they never saw fit to introduce the legislation to which all of us were sympathetic.
I believe Canadians as a whole feel quite badly about the fact that some men who suffered just as grave hardships as anyone else during the war years, and who should be entitled to assistance under the War Veterans' Allowance Act and other veterans' legislation, are denied that opportunity now. I am satisfied quite a number of families and young men gave up their lives in the struggle for the Atlantic. They are memorials to the fact that these people certainly did undergo every hardship that one could picture. For that reason, I would plead with the minister to give them the consideration they warrant.
As recently as June of this year the plight of the merchant seamen was drawn to the attention of the Prime Minister when he was in London. I have here a facsimile of a letter in which he replied to their request for some consideration.
While it was not so straightforward in its reply as was the former one, certainly it would give one hopes that the door was not shut and that the present minister would see fit to do something about it. I recognize that the Minister of Veterans Affairs is sympathetic to their cause. As I said earlier, I mention the matter with the hope that he will draw to the attention of his colleagues in the cabinet the need for the inclusion of these merchant seamen. The fact that so many members of the house support this plea might make it a little bit easier for him to get the inclusion of these merchant seamen past the treasury board so that something could be done to assist them.
The other question that I have in mind is one which I consider is a serious one. In fact, it arises out of a letter to a news editor which appeared in the Western Producer of April 4, 1957. It is signed by Kenneth Winter, Merid, Saskatchewan. The charges in this case, to my mind, are very serious and I believe that they should be given further consideration, possibly with a view to discussing the matter with the officials of the Saskatchewan government in order to see whether something could not be done to assist these people or to prevent what this war veteran charges is actually taking place. I am not going to read the full letter because some of it is not too complimentary to the present C.C.F. government in Saskatchewan. The pertinent part of it reads as follows:
However, in Saskatchewan where they are in control,-
That is the C.C.F.
-their attitude in dealing with their own tanners is slightly different. Saskatchewan crown land

is leased to veterans on long term leases, also to non-veterans. The federal government through the V.L.A. extends assistance to veterans to purchase machinery to break and work this land. The veteran pays a smaller than usual share of crop as rental directly to the Saskatchewan government. Also, contrary to the usual procedure where the landlord pays the taxes, the veteran is responsible for taxes. Thus the taxes are actually part of the rental. If the farmer has a total crop failure, naturally that part of the rental which is crop share would be nothing, but the taxes still are required to be paid.
Thus the veteran really has a cash rental in the form of taxes to pay even if he doesn't harvest a bushel. Last fall, every holder of a veteran's lease on crown land received a letter from the Saskatchewan government (the landlord), stating emphatically that if any rural municipality reported taxes unpaid on a veteran's lease, the government would automatically cancel that lease. This is the most vicious system of merciless collection in existence. I do not believe any other landlord but the C.C.F. government could get away with it-a cash payment on the barrel head every year, crop or no crop. After years of picking rock and clearing and breaking land, a crop failure or delivery restrictions could cause a veteran to fall behind on his taxes-then, wham, the landlord (the C.C.F. government) cancels his lease and unless the unfortunate veteran could get more land to farm, no doubt he would lose his machinery to the V.L.A.
It is much easier for a veteran to lose his lease than for an established farmer to lose his land through the tax enforcement act, by which a tax lien must first be filed. This winter all holders of grazing leases on crown land who owed all or part of the 1956 rental, received a letter stating that as their rental was six weeks overdue, their leases would be cancelled unless the department heard from the renter within 30 days.
It carries on further but that is all it has to say with respect to the veteran and this particular problem. I would urge the minister and the department officials-
I wonder if I might ask the hon. member from what document he is reading?

As I said earlier, I am reading from a copy of a letter which was reproduced in the Western Producer open forum, Regina and Ottawa. It is a letter signed by Kenneth Winter, Merid, Saskatchewan and apparently dated April 4, 1957.
I recognize that the municipality must get its taxes as must any government. I am not suggesting for one moment that the Saskatchewan government should necessarily pay the taxes to a municipality for a veteran who is not in a position to do so. There is a definite problem there. But I feel that it is up to our Department of Veterans Affairs which has authority in this matter to discuss it with the officials of the Saskatchewan government in order to see whether we cannot work out a scheme whereby this matter could be settled more amicably.

Mr. Chairman, this is going to be a wee speech. May I join with other hon. members
Supply-Veterans Affairs in extending congratulations to the Minister of Veterans Affairs on the excellent manner in which he and his officers are administering the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Might I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.
Why does he appear today in the national costume of his youth?
What is that again? Why do I appear in the kilt today?
Yes.
I will come to that matter just in a moment or two.
Will you answer that question "What is a kilt?" That is something we should all like to know.
Is it true what they say about Scots in kilts?

Mr. Chairman, already today I have had quite a few questions on the kilt, but I cannot let them go into Hansard.
It is a pleasure to follow the hon. member who spoke immediately before the hon. member who just sat down and whose speech indicates that he comes from the land of the heather. I refer to the hon. member for Selkirk.
Today is the eve of the feast of St. Andrew, patron saint of Scotland, and of all sons of Scotland throughout the world. Tomorrow Scots everywhere will follow the skirl of the pipes and the swirl of the kilt to partake of the traditional food of our ancestors-the haggis. Then will follow the songs of the immortal Robert Burns and others equally renowned; and the highland fling, sword dance, seann thruibhas, followed by the oft-repeated stories of our ancestors until the wee small hours of the morning.

I would like to add my voice to those who have already given their congratulations to the hon. minister upon his appointment as Minister of Veterans Affairs and I feel sure that under his capable guidance the veterans will be well looked after. I also wish to thank him for the amendments he has already brought before the house, particularly those affecting Newfoundland and to add at this time my support to the arguments made this afternoon by my colleague, the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, a veteran who served in world war I and also in world war II.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
I also had a copy of this brief forwarded to me by Mr. W. R. Martin, the provincial secretary, Newfoundland Command of the Canadian Legion, British Empire Service League. I will not go into this in detail as was done by my colleague, but would like to say that it has my heartiest support and that I trust the minister will, either by regulations or if that is not possible, by necessary legislation, satisfy the arguments contained in this brief. I particularly hope that he will introduce before this house such legislation as will put the veterans of Newfoundland on a par with the rest of the Canadian veterans. I know at the time when veterans affairs were considered by those who arranged the terms of confederation with Newfoundland in 1947 and 1948, it was recognized that there would no doubt be certain items which would come up in future years and which would have to be straightened out. I feel sure that the hon. minister, who comes from one of the Atlantic provinces, will recognize the claims of Newfoundlanders in this regard and I think we can rely upon him to do anything necessary in order to solve the problems faced by those in that part of the country.
Before I sit down I would also like to indicate my support with those members who have already spoken on the matter of the merchant marine. Coming as I do from Newfoundland and living close to the Atlantic ocean I feel we are in a position to know the great work those men performed in peacetime, and particularly in wartime, in keeping open the channels of transportation by which we have been able to provide the necessary food to keep our population from starvation. I cannot speak too strongly in support of all necessary measures which can be taken in the interests of the veterans and merchant marine and if the minister feels there is any additional legislation which should be brought before this house I feel sure it will be given very sympathetic consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to join in paying tribute to the hon. Minister of Veterans Affairs. His regard for veterans has been well known over the period of his service in this house and I know his sincerity and good will is unquestioned. I feel sure he has the support and confidence of all veterans organizations.
There are, however, two matters which I would like to bring before the committe which have been spoken to by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo and the hon. member for New Westminster, and which concern nearly all members who come from seaports or from areas adjacent to the seas which


border this land. This first subject to which I refer is the merchant marine.
I do wish the minister would take into consideration those men who in their service have battled a battle with no time out. I refer to the battle of the Atlantic which did not stop; there was pressure all the time and danger all the time. Their casualties in proportion to their numbers were, I believe, as high as those suffered by any of the fighting services in the second world war and his late majesty, King George VI, recognized the courage and devotion of the merchant marine by designating it the merchant navy, and gave it the distinction of being called the fourth arm of the fighting forces. These men received no re-establishment grants, no V.L.A. payments or gratuities but they gave outstanding service. I do not think it is fair to consider them in the same category as the firefighters or to say that the minister will have opened the door for a large number of other groups to receive the benefits of the War Veterans' Allowance Act. I think the merchant seamen could quite rightly be classed in the same way as the veterans of the army, the air force and the navy.
As I said when I commenced to speak, there is a second point about which I would like to say a few words and that is, if you will permit a little pun, rank discrimination. These remarks have to do with that part of the Pension Act which deals with what are called supplementary pensions. As is well known, Canada had no air service before or during the first world war and therefore a Canadian who desired to join a flying service had to join one of the imperial forces either the Royal Naval Air Service or the Royal Flying Corps. If he was an officer in the Canadian forces he was, with the consent of his commanding officer, seconded for duty with either of the above mentioned flying services, retaining the rank he held in the Canadian forces but in all other respects taking a junior position in the new services. He was paid by the Canadian government at a consolidated rate of pay, equal to the rate of pay in the new service. On the return of this officer to Canada he was treated entirely as a Canadian, both for the purposes of gratuity and pension. If pensioned he could draw such either in or out of Canada and he would not come under supplementary pension regulations.
Now if you compare the seconded officer's position as set forth with that which would apply to an individual-not an officer-who was in the ranks of the Canadian army and wished to join the same flying service, this individual would, with the consent of his commanding officer, be discharged from the Canadian army and would then be taken on

by the imperial flying services and commissioned. After his service and on his return to Canada he would be treated as an imperial in regard to gratuity and pension and would be allowed to draw Canadian rates of pension upon proof of residence in Canada at the date of August 4, 1914. He could draw the supplementary pension under the act only if he continued to live in Canada, and not even medical opinion would suffice to allow him to go abroad to live and still receive it.
As 1 said before, that is rank discrimination. The same treatment should be accorded to the non-commissioned officer or the private who joined the Royal Flying Corps or the Royal Naval Air Service as would be accorded to him if he had held a commission and had been seconded to those services. I do wish the minister would take this matter into consideration. I do not believe it would involve a great deal of trouble to recognize the facts; there cannot be too many people concerned but it is not right to leave things in that way.

Mr. Chairman, I am going to be very brief in my remarks. We have a problem which concerns veterans in Medicine Hat and as a matter of fact it is the number one problem there in so far as the veterans and the branch of the Canadian Legion are concerned.
This problem arises out of the offering for sale of houses in what is known as the Medicine Hat project No. 38 which is 100 per cent occupied by veterans. These sale prices were set at an amount almost 100 per cent of the initial cost in spite of the fact that these are frame buildings and are almost 10 years old.
Now the total cost including payments for land and so on, according to information I have received from one of the departments here was, $722,114 and, also according to this information, the anticipated recovery from the sale of these houses is $710,500, or very nearly 100 per cent of the initial cost plus the cost of the land, which of course would have to be paid to municipalities as soon as they are sold. This does not, however, take into consideration the fact that $365,000 has been paid in rentals during the period from 1948 to 1957. Surely any reasonable person would have to agree that there must be some depreciation on a frame building over a ten-year period.
Having had to pay 100 per cent of the initial cost this deal ties the veterans down for the next 25 years at these high prices and with a 6 per cent interest rate.
I will admit, as the veterans do, that the maintenance, appearance and general value
Supply-Veterans Affairs of these buildings has been kept at a high level during these years but I would like the members of this committee to know that the main reason for this is that the veterans have taken money out of their own pockets to pay for interior decorating, landscaping and in fact everything that was necessary in the way of maintenance with the exception of major replacements such as a hot water tank or some other significant purchase.
I do not want to speak on this subject at great length because I intend to bring it up in more detail when the estimates of the Department of Public Works are brought in. Since this is a matter that is of concern only to veterans I would urge the Minister of Veterans Affairs to look into it. I would like him to study the picture, the arrangements for financing over the 25-year period and the other details and then decide if he thinks it is fair to ask these veterans to pay back all the money that was expended to construct the project. They have regularly paid their rent throughout the years and as I said this amounted to $365,000 so it is obvious that there is a substantial profit some place. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation advise me they are not actually making a profit on these buildings but they have not as yet been able to show me what has happened to the $365,000.
On June 11, 1956, an hon. member asked what was the amount of expenditure on the upkeep of this project for painting, repairs, etc. up to March 31, 1956. The answer was $17,995. It was also asked what was the cost of administration up to the same period and the answer was $22,350. This represents only a very small portion of the $365,000. I realize of course there was some interest that had to be paid on the original capital investment but even with a reasonable rate of interest and taking into consideration the maintenance and administration the cost would not come anywhere near the amount that was paid in rent. There must be a profit some place but I do not know where. If Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has not made any money on this project then one can only conclude that some money has been transferred. I do not know where it has been transferred to, but I think a large part of it should be applied to depreciation. If that were done the asking price for these houses could be lowered. This would satisfy the Canadian Legion and the veterans who are living in these houses.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say only a few words at this time but before doing so I wish to express my appreciation to the officials to the Department of Veterans Affairs. In the short time I have been here
1688	HOUSE OF
Supply-Veterans Affairs I have referred a number of problems to them and have been extremely pleased with the kind reception I have received.
I would like to refer for a moment to the work that is being done under the Veterans' Land Act and the amount of information and assistance that is being given to young farmers under this act which is certainly appreciated by the farmers concerned. I think it would be advisable for the department to again take a look at the prices that are being paid for land because in some cases the prices that are being offered by the department are unrealistic in my opinion. However, it may be that revaluations have not been made to date but are in the process of being made.
Another matter the department should keep in mind is one I raised previously regarding insurance for service personnel. I believe we should adopt a system similar to that used in the last war by the United States government of carrying an insurance policy of $20,000 to $25,000 on service personnel so their dependants would receive some assistance in the event of the death of a veteran or one who is hurt or maimed during hours when he is not covered, at the present time, by the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Certainly all Canadians are proud of what we were able to give our service personnel following the war in terms of the equality we were able to establish between what they had before giving their service and what they received upon return to civilian life. We would like to constantly improve conditions for our service personnel and this could be done quite effectively if the government would put into the pay structure an amount to cover the premium on a paid-up insurance policy on a term basis of $20,000 to $25,000. For instance, in the case of one of our service personnel serving in a foreign country who was killed in an automobile accident while off duty, the adoption of such a plan would provide his dependants with something to tide them over in that time of need. It may be argued that this is not the responsibility of the government and that the service personnel are aware of such eventualities and should make provision accordingly, but this thought is of small comfort and no compensation to the wife and family of a member of the services who dies in circumstances such as those I have outlined. I urge the minister to give consideration to this suggestion and I would hope that it would be adopted.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the minister one question. Will the government consider the granting of pensions without a means test at age 60 to veterans who have served in active warfare?

Mr. Chairman, I have several observations to make with respect to veterans legislation. I realize the desirability of proceeding as soon as possible with the consideration of the actual estimates. However, I might just mention several matters with respect to veterans legislation. I believe that the veterans across the cor itry are experiencing an increased sense o. satisfaction with the legislation which is being brought in from time to time, much of if to clear up some of the ambiguity that existed. Other measures were introduced to close some of the gaps in the legislative program, and I do know that the veterans are very pleased with the interest taken by members of parliament in these particular matters.
I should like to refer once again to the position in which some of the veterans find themselves when, although they are in receipt of war veterans allowances, they are not able to supplement their income through casual earnings. There are various factors which contribute to this situation. It may be a health factor, or else the economic situation of the area in which they are residing, and they find it impossible to supplement their incomes in any other way. These veterans are still finding themselves in a very serious position economically, and I feel that real consideration should be given to the matter to try to improve the lot of veterans in this category. I believe there is disappointment over the fact that there is no increase in the basic pension; but there are several other factors which I would like to mention in connection with pensions. One was raised by the hon. member for Acadia. It was the Legion's request as follows:
Where a pension applicant who served in an actual theatre of war is found to have a disability resulting from an injury or a disease not recorded on medical examination prior to enlistment, such injury or disease shall be presumed to have occurred or had its inception subsequent to enlistment.
Now, I feel in this particular respect many of the veterans are suffering from a very serious injustice. I believe that the Legion is taking only a very sensible attitude to the situation in making the request that this particular matter be clarified. I am not saying that the pension board would deliberately use this particular loophole to deprive an individual of his right to pension or the benefits that should be his; but I do feel that the legislation should be opened up to the extent that the pension board itself possibly could exercise more initiative and consider the applications on their merits rather than just being held to a strict and severe interpretation of the letter of the law. This is one of

the matters which I would bring once again to the attention of the minister and his department.
In connection with the awarding of pensions, I have been approached by at least one of my constituents not too long ago relative to this very matter. An application has been made but time has slipped by for months, in fact for years, possibly, and then finally the pension board awarded the pension to the individual but there is no provision for a retroactive award. I do not think it is quite fair that a person who qualifies for benefits in this way should be placed in the position where, after a period of months or even years, he loses the benefits because of the fact that the particular application had not been processed satisfactorily up to that time. I do feel that this matter should be given consideration. I know that the Legion in their brief refer to this matter as well. On page 14 of the brief presented to the Prime Minister of Canada and the cabinet by the Canadian Legion we find section 7 dealing with retroactive awards. The Legion says:
We would advocate that it be made mandatory that when a decision is given favourable to the veteran, pension will be paid as of date of application.
The brief goes on to record the possible difficulties of establishing whether or not the person is eligible, but once he is declared to be eligible, then I feel the award should be made retroactive. I believe the Legion is very modest in its request in this regard because, on page 16, it states:
This provision shall not apply to claims granted prior to January 1, 1946, and no retroactive payments shall be made for a period prior to that date.
It just means that the applicants who made their applications back at that time have no means of redress, and apparently they are just out of the benefits. However, I do trust that the minister will give his attention to this matter.
These are the only matters to which I wish to call attention at this time, Mr. Chairman. The rest can be dealt with as we proceed with the estimates.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be exceedingly brief this afternoon because two of my colleagues have already spoken at some length in putting before the committee the pleadings of this group in regard to this very important matter. However, I should like to express my feelings in regard to one very important aspect of pensions for veterans. I have had a number of cases brought to my attention having to do with the failure of a veteran to receive a pension Eor service owing to the fact that he could lot prove that his disability occurred during
Supply-Veterans Affairs service. I want to add my voice to that of those hon. members who have already seen fit to bring this matter to, the attention of the minister.
The hon. member for Kootenay West said earlier today that it would not take too much money to give further justice to the veterans of the first and second world wars. Many of the injustices of the past have been cleared up but I think, sir, that one of the most important things is the psychological effect on a veteran who has given service to his country, has come back and is unable to care for himself and his family when he finds that for some reason he is not eligible for a service pension. On occasions it has been pointed out to me that such a veteran, if he is indigent, can apply to the commission and get the war veterans allowance. I think, sir, that justice comes first and if the veteran has served, as have the individuals who have been brought to my attention, and for whom I have been fighting with the commission to try to get some type of eligibility for pension, then he should receive a pension. I do not think it is sufficient to say that that man can get war veterans allowance in lieu of entitlement to a legitimate veterans pension.
The point is this, Mr. Chairman, as is well known by all members in the chamber. If a veteran enlisted in either world war I or world war II, was classified as A-l and then was discharged, not demobilized, with a disability, surely it must be admitted that the disability was due to service and the onus of proof must be on the pension commission to prove that the disability was not in fact caused by his service. That is the point I wish to make.
I have some case histories here and I should like to refer to one. I am not going to use the veteran's name, but this man enlisted and after examination by specialists was given an A-l category. He had service in the first great war. When he was discharged he was in E category. It is well known that with an E category he should have been automatically boarded for his disability, but this veteran has been fighting to try to get a pension for his disability. He was discharged because of arthritis of the spine. His medical case history indicates that the disease or injury was arthritis of the spine, that the place of origin was unknown and the date of origin was unknown.
Surely we as members of the house do not have to continue to fight for justice for such veterans. I hope that the rumours I have heard are true that the government in the future will be more tolerant towards veterans making application for pension. I hope that members will not have to fight interminably

Supply-Veterans Affairs for such veterans. If a veteran had an A-l category when he entered one of the services after inspection by the medical officials and came out with a low category which necessitated his discharge, surely in the name of justice such a veteran should get a pension.
I only hope that very soon all the outstanding cases that come before us and the pension commission will receive justice, that the onus of proof will, if necessary, be placed on the commission rather than on the veteran to prove the disability and that justice will be given to such veterans.

I wish to say a few words in answer to the questions raised by different hon. members. First I want to thank them most sincerely for their very kind remarks with reference to myself and particularly with reference to my staff. I wish to thank the hon. member for Rosthern. I think he was the first to mention this very important matter, and I can assure him that the feelings he expressed regarding my staff are the same as my own and for the same reason.
The hon. member for Kootenay West and the hon. member for Acadia, who have been in the house for many years and have been members of veterans affairs committees with myself, made, along with others, many recommendations. I appreciate very much the recommendations that have been made. They are not new. They have been made many times before. It simply goes to show that veterans problems are always with us and that while we may make amendments to the legislation at one session or in one year there is still unfinished business which has to be dealt with later.
The hon. members mentioned particularly the merchant navy and the firefighters. The hon. member for Kootenay West, the hon. member for Acadia and also the hon. member for Selkirk, who has been in the house for a number of years, will remember that these problems were discussed on numerous occasions in the past. When the veterans charter was being considered we had the advice of many veterans organizations across Canada. The merchant marine representatives and also the representatives of the firefighters appeared before us.
From conversations I have had with some of the new members I am of the opinion that many of them think there is is no legislation dealing with the firefighters and the merchant marine, but I should like to point out to them that in the firefighters act, which they will find in the veterans charter, many benefits have already been bestowed upon the firefighters. The same applies to the merchant marine and a number of other groups which were also considered at the same time.

One of the great problems we have encountered, and which was encountered when I was a member of the committee, is the fact that neither the merchant marine nor the corps of firefighters were considered to be part of the armed forces, and some of the advantages and benefits which they are asking now were denied them and have been denied them throughout the years on that account. That is a problem which still requires considerable attention and discussion. It is one of the matters which should claim the attention of a veterans affairs committee when such a committee is set up.
I want to assure the hon. member for Selkirk that it is my intention to have a veterans affairs committee set up at the next session of parliament. I made that very clear, I thought, when the war veterans allowance amendments were before the house a short time ago. I believe the hon. member for Acadia also mentioned section 13 of the Pension Act which has to do with pre-enlistment disabilities. This is also a subject which has been discussed in the house and in the committee on many occasions and it also requires further study. There is also the matter of the benefit of the doubt. The hon. member for Acadia will remember that we did not spend hours but days discussing this matter when it was before the committee in days gone by, and in his opinion and the opinion of many others it is still a matter that is not settled. Certainly it is not settled to the satisfaction of a great many and will still require attention.
The hon. member for Acadia spoke about the case of the widow in Winnipeg who should, in his opinion, receive a pension. I am sure he will be glad to know that the chairman of the pension commission will be pleased to look into the matter and give it further attention. I was very pleased to hear some hon. members give praise to the administration of the Veterans' Land Act. I have heard considerable praise of the administration of the act and I may say I was very pleased about two weeks ago to have the opportunity to meet the district superintendents from all across Canada, the men who are responsible for the administration of the act throughout the dominion.
Judging by the calibre of the men who came here to Ottawa three weeks ago, I would say that the administration of this act was in good hands all across this country. It is known to me, and I think it is known to hon. members here that the men who have settled under the Veterans' Land Act are taking a very leading part in the communities in which they live. We are very proud of that. They are certainly making a great contribution throughout this country.

There was a question asked regarding the corps of commissionaires by the hon. member for Acadia. The corps of commissionaires is an independent body, with its own board of directors, and it operates within all provinces. The hon. member for York-Sunbury, who was an executive of the Canadian Legion, was quite correct in his explanation. The commissionaires are employees of the corps and not of the government. The government employs some commissionaires, as a matter of fact about 50 per cent of those who are employed. In the case of private employers the rate is set by arrangement between the corps and the employers. When the government employ commissionaires, the rate is set by the treasury board on the basis of the prevailing rate for that area. I believe the rate differs across Canada and in some sections it is lower than in others. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that explains to hon. members the situation with regard to the corps of commissionaires.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo mentioned the Newfoundland problem. This is a problem which is peculiar to Newfoundland, and it is one which is being studied at the present time and one which will have to be very carefully studied when the committee is set up.
The hon. member for Selkirk brought up the question of the mentally sick. He asked if pensions were paid during mental illness. They are paid, and they are used for the benefit of the dependants of the mentally ill person.
If the patient is receiving a pension when he goes into hospital, does he get the whole of the pension or just a percentage of it?
The whole of the pension is paid.
He gets the whole pension?

Yes. The hon. member for New Westminster mentioned the merchant seamen. I might say in that connection that there is no one who appreciates what the merchant seamen suffered and the contribution they made to the winning of the war more than I do. We know of the terrific hardships they experienced, and we know also of the heavy casualties which they suffered. The hon. member for New Westminster asked for a further study of the situation concerning children of the war dead, and I can assure him that will be done. I believe the hon. member for Vancouver South was also interested in the merchant seamen. The hon. member for Medicine Hat mentioned the sale of land under the Veterans' Land Act, and
Supply-Veterans Affairs this is a problem to which we shall have to give careful study before I can make any definite statement.
The hon. member for Timiskaming mentioned the Veterans' Land Act and I wish to thank him for the praise he gave the administrators of that act. He spoke about the information and assistance which was given to young farmers. He thought the price paid for farms was continually rising, and this is a matter, of course, which would have to be looked into. The hon. member also mentioned the insurance on serving personnel. This does not come under the Department of Veterans Affairs, but under the Department of National Defence.
I do not wish to take any more time. The individual items will be considered, and if there are any more questions which hon. gentlemen wish to ask we will do our best to answer them.
The minister did not comment on the question I raised concerning the enlisted men who had been discharged to serve in the royal flying corps as compared with officers who had been seconded.
Will the hon. gentleman be satisfied if we write and give him the full explanation? There is quite a long story to that.

It might facilitate the passing of the actual items of the estimates if the minister were to indicate whether or not he is recommending these estimates as they are found in the blue book or whether he is making any changes. If he finds the estimates satisfactory and there is no waste or extravagance, and is recommending them as they were brought in by the previous government and as studied by the estimates committee, then that might facilitate their passage. These estimates are very familiar to the members of that committee.

I might say to the hon. member that I am recommending them as they are set out in the book. So far as waste and extravagance is concerned, at the beginning of his speech the hon. member wanted to know from me whether or not I considered there was waste and extravagance in the department. I might say at once that I have not found any waste or extravagance, but T did not expect to find them in this department. This department deals almost entirely with pensions, war veterans' allowances and many thousands of things which the hon. member mentioned in his speech. There is not any chance for waste and the money spent for our veterans could not in any way be considered waste or extravagance.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
So far as the construction of our buildings is concerned, that is another matter altogether. This is looked after by another department and I have no intention of answering so far as that is concerned.

Item agreed to.
Treatment services-
500. Operation of hospitals and administration, including authority for payments, during the current and subsequent fiscal years, to canteen funds of departmental hospitals in amounts equal to the amounts of commissions received by or on behalf of Her Majesty from pay telephones in such hospitals, $44,368,445.

I do not intend to delay the committee long but I want to raise a matter that I promised certain patients of Shaugh-nessy hospital to raise, certain veterans I have met, certain dependants who have written to me about this matter and certain Legion members who were at Legion meetings and who discussed it while I was present. I understand that under our regulations certain veterans, other than those who go into hospitals for their war disabilities and those in receipt of war veterans' allowance, are entitled to enter our hospitals provided they make certain satisfactory arrangements in relation to their financial circumstances. I understand if a veteran cannot meet the regulations of the department, then the officials-I know they do their best in this respect-make every effort possible to see they are properly provided for under the auspices of the provincial authorities concerned.
This matter first came to my notice when I was visiting Shaughnessy hospital when a number of patients took strong exception to the fact that they had comrades knocking on the door who could not get in because of the regulations while male immigrants were receiving hospital services, dentures, glasses and all other things that were required and certain female immigrants and children were getting a sort of out-patient service. We know that these people must be cared for but I remember very well when the late Hon. Ian Mackenzie dedicated Shaughnessy hospital and spoke at the opening of the hospital. At that time he said that this hospital was built to serve the needs of the veterans and the men who fought for this country. I am not blaming the minister or the department for these circumstances but I take strong exception, as do a good many Canadians, to the fact that there are veterans who fought for this country who are in needy circumstances and who, under our regulations, can be denied admission to veterans hospitals. I will admit


arrangements will be made with the provincial authorities to care for them. We know that people who are ill must be cared for.
I understand that the department-and I judge this from some conversations that I have had at lower levels-rather reluctantly complies with the wishes of the immigration department. This matter that arose in Shaughnessy hospital came to a head, shall I say, rather as a result of the influx of Hungarians whom I prefer to call on the whole freedom seekers. I met some of the boys in there and they are quite stirred up about the matter. One of them told me that there was actually in the hospital a patient who had fought against this country, while he had a chum who needed treatment but who could not get in under the regulations. I think the situation should be the other way around. I think our immigration department should make arrangements with the provincial authorities and other hospital institutions for the care of those people because they pay for those services and that not a single needy veteran who requires treatment should be denied treatment in a veterans affairs hospital in this country at this time. These hospitals were erected and are maintained for that particular purpose.
I could speak at considerable length on this matter because I have had a good many representations in connection with it. I am rising to bring this matter to the attention of the minister at the request of some of my comrades in British Columbia and in my constituency. I should like the minister to inform the house of the numbers of immigrants who have been admitted to veterans hospitals in Canada during the past year and the numbers of Canadian veterans who have been denied admission under the regulations, and of the arrangements that are made by the immigration department for these free services to immigrants.

I am rather surprised to hear of this complaint from Shaughnessy. I think I can assure the hon. member immediately that there were no veterans refused admission to Shaughnessy hospital. That is my information. As to the number of Hungarians admitted, we have not that information before us, but I will get it and see that the hon. member receives it. However, I know that in the Ste-Foy hospital in Quebec a request was made that some of the Hungarian immigrants be admitted to the hospital and I know that every care was taken to see that our veterans were not denied beds in that hospital before any Hungarians or any one else was admitted to the hospital. That is the policy of the department. This is my first information

Supply-Veterans Affairs
that the policy has not always been carried out. However, if the hon. member will supply us with the particulars we will certainly see that there is an investigation in this connection.

I should like to ask the minister a further question. Do I understand him correctly that no needy veteran- that is needy from a financial point of view -will ever be refused admission to a veterans affairs hospital in Canada?
No eligible veteran.
Pardon me; a distinction is made. What does the minister mean by the term "eligible"?
Under our treatment regulations provision is made for eligible veterans.

That is my point. There are veterans who are not eligible under our regulations, and who can be denied admission at the present time. I suggest that no needy or destitute veteran in Canada, regardless of the present regulations, should be denied admission when we can make provision for other persons.

Item agreed to.
Miscellaneous payments-
510. To provide for payment to the last post fund: for the payment under regulations of funeral and cemetery charges, including the perpetual care of graves where applicable; for the cost and erection of headstones in Canada; for the maintenance of departmental cemeteries; for the maintenance of Canadian battlefields memorials in France and Belgium and for Canada's share of the expenditures of the Imperial war graves commission, $1,378,800.

May I have from the minister an explanation as to what extent this item 510 applies, the extent of funeral plots under perpetual care, the extent of headstones that are erected across the country and what are the requirements for obtaining those.
Does the hon. member refer to the last post fund?
Yes.

The Last Post Fund Incorporated. This vote covers certain expenses incurred by or provided for by the Department of Veterans Affairs in respect of burials and memorials. An explanation of the various administrative functions, cost of which is provided for herein, is as follows. The Last Post Fund Incorporated operates under a dominion charter for the purpose of preventing the burial of a veteran in a pauper's grave. Veteran, for the purpose of the regulations, means a former member of our armed forces. There are certain amounts paid. As to funerals and cemetery charges, under the veterans
burial regulations the department is authorized to arrange and pay for the funeral and burial of certain veterans who died while on treatment strength of the department, but only when no other person or agency will accept final responsibility therefor. For a funeral, the department may pay an amount not exceeding $175 for the services of one funeral director or $225 when the services of two funeral directors are necessary and are provided. In addition to funeral costs the department is authorized to pay certain cemetery charges and to provide a grave. That is the general principle under which we operate. I wonder whether that answers the hon. member's question.
Do I understand that it means that this is applied to those veterans under treatment who are going to come under that pauper section?

If they die under treatment in our hospitals or while on treatment strength they are looked after by our department under this particular vote. If they die outside, they are looked after under the last post fund to which we make contibutions.

Item agreed to.
Soldier Settlement and Veterans' Land Act-
516. To provide for the cost of administration of Veterans' Land Act; soldier settlement and British family settlement, $5,029,545.
I wonder whether the minister could give us what is the deadline for applications under the Veterans' Land Act.
There is no deadline.

I wonder whether I got the minister's answer correctly. I have had one or two veterans say to me that the expiry date under which they might receive money under the Veterans' Land Act is soon to be reached. I think perhaps this is in relation to re-establishment credit which they might receive and which they might have to pay back. I am not an authority on this bill but veterans have spoken to me and they were under the impression that they had very little time remaining during which they might receive money under the Veterans' Land Act for the purchase of homes. If they are under any misapprehension I am sure they would be very pleased to have reassurance from the minister.
The hon. member has referred to the deadline for the re-establishment credit, that is 1960. There is a deadline there.

Item agreed to.

The house in committee on Bill No. 18, respecting the British Columbia Telephone Company-Mr. Jung-Mr. Casselman in the chair.
On clause 1-Repeal.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to discuss this bill at length in the committee of the whole. The standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, of course, was the scene of some detailed discussion. In view of the rather complicated nature of some of the evidence given by the officials of the company in the standing committee it is perhaps unfortunate that the proceedings of that committee reached the mail boxes of hon. members of the house only today which means we have not had an opportunity to properly study and analyse the verbal representations made in the standing committee by the officers of the company.
As far as those members of that committee who sit in the C.C.F. corner of the house are concerned we did recognize and were satisfied as a result of the evidence given by the officials in the committee that there is need for a considerable capital expansion program in the telephone services in the province of British Columbia. Certainly many of us who represent constituencies in that province and who are receiving constant information from our constituents about their desire and need for an extension of the existing telephone facilities hardly needed to be told that by the officials of the company.
The position of the C.C.F. group in respect to the British Columbia Telephone Company has been well known over the years in the province of British Columbia. We feel that this being a monopoly public utility in our province it should more properly come under public ownership and that if steps were taken to bring that about substantial savings to the telephone users of the province of British Columbia could result.
As I say, much of the evidence which was given by the company officials in the committee was rather complicated, at least as far as a layman like myself-in matters of high finance-is concerned, but I think there were one or two facts which became generally apparent as a result of that discussion. One was the fact that this company which in the province of British Columbia is known as the British Columbia Telephone Company is in fact not a British Columbia telephone company at all but it is a company which is in part owned and in fact controlled by United States financial interests. That information given by the company's officers as

a result of a little prodding here and there during the course of the questioning coupled with the facts relating to the interrelationship between the parent company and the British Columbia Telephone Company and some of the concerns which are engaged in supplying telephone equipment does reveal that there is a great possibility that under various arrangements unnecessary costs are entering into the picture in the province of British Columbia as far as telephone rates are concerned. That is to say, when the board of transport commissioners reviews the applications of the company, because of this very complicated corporate structure that lies behind the carrying out of their operations there are as far as I was able to judge from the evidence given in the committee a good many possibilities that hidden costs and charges which of course have to be passed on to the users of telephone services within the province of British Columbia will not be revealed.
As I said when I rose, Mr. Chairman, it is not my desire to discuss this matter at length but I did feel I should report to the committee of the whole at least those conclusions I arrived at after having sat in the committee meetings during the presentation of the evidence by the company. I can assure the committee of the whole and possibly also the British Columbia Telephone Company that those of us who come from the province of British Columbia and are elected to this house under the banner of the C.C.F. certainly intend to continue to pay a great deal of attention to the operation of this company.
In a province such as British Columbia where many of the communities are separated by long distances and where modes of travel in many cases are limited the type of telephone service that is provided is a very vital concern to the people who live there. Certainly this is true in respect to many of the people who live in the more isolated areas along the coast, a large part of which falls within the boundaries of the constituency of Comox-Alberni. I know that many af the people who live in those areas are not satisfied with the service they are getting at the present time. Rightly or wrongly they nave the feeling that this telephone company whose primary concern is the making of profits for its shareholders has been inclined '.o concentrate upon the richest fields of en-ieavour, that is the more heavily populated areas in the lower mainland of the province. They feel that because of the primary concern of this privately owned utility in the naking of profits for its shareholders services are not as good as they might otherwise be.
On the other hand from suggestions I have leard made by some of my colleagues who
Private Bills
live in the more heavily populated areas I understand that some of their constituents also feel there is room for improvement in the service provided by this company and that in many cases they feel the rates they are paying for the service are higher than they think they should be paying.
As we indicated at the second reading stage of this bill, we realize that basically the bill is not concerned with the form or type of ownership of our telephone system in the province of British Columbia and the passage or otherwise of this bill is not going to give us an opportunity to bring about the changes we would like to see made. I think we made it clear that we had no desire in any way to prevent the British Columbia Telephone Company from being able to finance the carrying out of the services that are needed in many of the growing areas of the province and after having heard the evidence given in the committee I think I can say we hold substantially the same views we expressed on second reading and we are not at all happy about some of the indications that were revealed as a result of the questions we asked in the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to congratulate the hon. member on presenting his bill and I hope he will be successful in piloting it through the house. I would like to ask him one or two questions. Are there any independent, provincial or municipal telephone systems in the province of British Columbia?

Mr. Chairman, I believe there is one, the Okanagan Telephone Company. There have been other telephone companies that have since been absorbed by the B.C. Telephone Company. The B.C. Telephone Company purchased the Mission Telephone Company Limited in 1952, and with that purchase the company expanded its territories by the addition of operations in the Fraser valley north of the Fraser river. Then, in 1953, the B.C. Telephone Company purchased the Kootenay Telephone Company Limited and that completed the expansion to the east Kootenay section of British Columbia. In the following year, 1954, the Chilliwack Telephone Company Limited was also purchased and in 1954 the government telephone and telegraph service was also taken over by the B.C. Telephone Company. Since taking over the government service substantial improvements have been made. There have been major conversions from magneto to battery sets, pending the installation of new equipment, which will enable automatic dial telephones to be put in. New offices have been installed and improvements of the distribution plant; that is, pole lines have been

Private Bills
rebuilt and extended. It is proposed that hundreds of thousands of dollars will be going into that area.

Can the hon. member tell us something about the comparative rates, say for a private phone of the independent company in the Okanagan which is, I believe, a municipal phone system, and those charged in similar areas by the B.C. Telephone Company?
That question, I think, was asked in committee but I do not see the answer printed in the proceedings.

It is not a municipal system; it is a privately owned system. Its rates are above those of the B.C. Telephone Company for equivalent service. I have a telephone in the Okanagan and a telephone in Vancouver and therefore I know.
I was not questioning th'~ information at all. Does the B.C. Telephone Company have to apply to the board of transport commissioners for permission to increase rates?
Yes, it does.
What is the history of its applications in the past?

They have all been subjected to most searching and exhaustive inquiry and they have always been granted. The board of transport commissioners does not, I believe, have any control over the type of service, but it does exercise indirect control through asking questions about its rate structure and the price of the equipmen which it purchases. It indirectly controls the service extended to the subscribers in that area.

How many applications
have there been for an increase in rates, say, over the past 15 years?
I am sorry, I cannot answer that question but I can secure the information for my hon. friend.
What is the basis upon which the board of transport commissioners grant the increase? In case an application is made, what do they take into consideration, costs and so forth?
I am sorry I cannot answer that question because I am not a member of the board of transport commissioners and I am afraid it is outside my sphere of knowledge.
What about the value of the stock of this private company on the market? Has it been on the increase or has it been increasing lately? I believe their shares are of a par value of $25?
I am sorry, I also cannot answer that question but I am quite sure if the hon. member will refer to the financial page of any of the newspapers he will find that information will be available.

What I want to know is whether or not the board of transport commissioners would take into consideration, when they were asked for an increase in rates, the amount of dividends which were being paid on the shares of this company?

Mr. Chairman, I am quite sure they would. I understand the reason why the hon. member is asking these questions but it does not fall within the report of this committee. I am quite sure the board of transport commissioners will inquire into all phases of the company's activities if an application is made.

I know they would inquire into it. They would probably have the information already. I was just wondering whether or not they would want to know what considerations went into it, as to whether the company was making sufficient profit on its stock as it is today and as to whether or not it requires some increase in its rates, based on the profits it was making. The other question I would like to ask the sponsor of the bill is whether or not there has ever been a provincial telephone company established in the province of British Columbia to carry on this public service under provincial control and thus any profits accruing out of the operation of this public service would go to the people of the province rather than into the hands of a private company?
As far as I know, Mr. Chairman, the answer is no.

Mr. Chairman, I think we all appreciate the great expansion that is required in telephone service in British Columbia. Because the B.C. Telephone Company controls over 90 per cent of the telephone business in British Columbia we understand its requirements in coming before this House of Commons at this time and asking for an increase in its capitalization. I feel sure, Mr. Chairman, because of the requirements of service and assistance in employment, no member in this house will place any obstacle in the way of this bill going through.
However, along with the statement that the telephone service and employment situation in British Columbia are such that this bill must go through, we also have the responsibility of drawing to the attention of the committee the situation which has developed in British Columbia, and also

throughout Canada, in so far as a communication monopoly is concerned. We also must raise the question, perhaps not for decision now but for investigation later, as to the intricacies and complications in the company's management and in its method of financing.
I do not raise the question in order to block this bill, but I do believe that hon. members and the public should take note of the information given in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines to the effect that it is the declared intention of the B.C. Telephone Company to issue new capital to be authorized by this bill to the present shareholders of the B.C. Telephone Company.
It will be done at a cost to present holders of shares between 5 per cent and 6 per cent less than the market value of British Columbia Telephony Company shares. If you sell at less than the market value somebody has got to pay and in the long run it can only be the consumer. I think it is wrong in principle that privileged persons or companies should have the right to buy shares at 5 per cent to 6 per cent less than the market price and then be in the privileged position of not having to pay any income tax because we have no such thing as a capital gains tax in our country.
I was most interested, Mr. Chairman, in reading a remarkable speech made by a member of the other place not on this bill but on one of a similar nature. In a speech that must have taken him over half an hour he pointed out the dangers of monopoly in communications services and made a suggestion which I believe should be repeated on the floor of the house so I am going to do so now. He suggested that there should be a joint committee of the other place and the House of Commons to make a thorough investigation of the set-up, in all its intricacies and machinations, of companies in the communications field.
It was clearly apparent from the evidence given before the standing committee of the house with respect to the British Columbia Telephone Company that there are terrific intricacies and machinations. For example, it is correct that the B. C. Telephone Company is mostly owned in Canada but there is one block of shares amounting to about 35J per cent, I believe, owned by the Anglo-Canadian Telephone Company with headquarters in Montreal. Who controls Anglo-Canadian? It is controlled in the United States. It was honestly admitted in the evidence before the committee that the B.C. Telephone Company does not do its own purchasing or installing. It uses a company that is owned wholly by
Private Bills
Anglo-Canadian Telephone Company and one-third of its purchases are from a company which is owned in the United States and again owned by the same company that indirectly controls the B.C. Telephone Company.
Here we have the situation of a company that has almost a virtual monopoly of the communications system in British Columbia, or 90 per cent of it, which, in the words of its own president, is controlled in the United States, does its purchasing and installation through a company owned wholly by Anglo-Canadian and controlled in the United States, and buys one-third of its equipment from a company which is owned in the United States which company is in turn owned by the same octopus. From the manufacturing to the purchasing, installing and service end we have a vicious circle, a circle which I honestly believe is of such a nature that if investigated thoroughly would show that the cream from the profits of the B.C. Telephone Company is being drained off by these other companies and that the people of British Columbia are paying rates for telephone service which the company can prove on the basis of its own operations but which are unfair because the public utilities commission does not take into account the draining off of profits by subsidiary companies.
I say, Mr. Chairman, that we are aware of the need of extension of service in British Columbia. We know that it requires money. We are not going to block the passage of the bill in any way but we do think very seriously that in accordance with the suggestion made the other day by a member of the other place it is high time that a thorough examination was made of all the intricacies and manipulations of communications companies, the tie-up of interlocking directorates and operations through subsidiary companies in order to be able to assure the people of British Columbia and Canada that they are not being, as I honestly believe they are, rooked by monopoly corporations in the communications field, the British Columbia Telephone Company in my own province and other telephone companies in other parts of Canada.

I should like to speak for two or three minutes on the bill. I was a member of the committee which considered it and what we have just heard shows how people can take different interpretations from the evidence put before them. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni said that under prodding he got certain information. It seemed to me that it was freely and factually given. So far as financing is concerned, the hon. member for Vancouver East talked about a 5 per cent to 6 per cent lower price through the use of rights. It was explained that it was not 5
